entries.title: 2 men wounded, 1 critically, in Chatham shooting
entries.summary: <p>A pair of men were wounded in a shooting Wednesday evening in Chatham, Chicago police said.</p><p>At about 7:45 p.m. in the 800 block of East 79th Street, two men were shot by another man, who had approached them before fleeing the scene on foot, according to police.</p><p>A 29-year-old man was shot in the face and taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in serious condition, police said.</p><p>A 44-year-old man suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was taken to the same hospital in critical condition.</p><p>Area 2 detectives are investigating. No suspect information has been released. </p>

entries.title: Colin Rea leads White Sox fan club among — gasp — Cubs players
entries.summary: <p>This might rub some <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> fans the wrong way, but Cubs players are rooting for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> — reliever Colin Rea, in particular.</p><p>“I’m rooting for them because I think it would be cool to be Cubs-White Sox in the World Series,” Rea told the Sun-Times.</p><p>No doubt, that would be cool. Of course, the Cubs would need to get there, too. But Rea also appreciates the way the Sox play.</p><p>“They play the game hard, and they do a lot of good things,” he said. “And they’ve turned things around quickly.”</p><p>Indeed, the Sox are looking to become the first team in major-league history to reach the postseason after losing 100-plus games in the three previous seasons, as well as the first to win its division after a 100-loss season. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/16/sputtering-white-sox-fall-out-of-al-central-lead-for-the-first-time-since-july-4-will-venable-tommy-pham-colson-montgomery-munetaka-murakami-sean-newcomb-anthony-kay-hagen-smith" >Sox fell out of first place Wednesday </a>with a 6-3 loss to the Guardians but are in wild-card position.</p><p>“I was watching that game today,” Rea said. “That was tough.”</p><p>He also was watching Saturday night in the ninth inning, when Randal Grichuk hit a two-strike, two-out pitch for a go-ahead two-run homer that gave the Sox a much-needed victory against the Cardinals.</p><p>“He did a good job where he kind of got beat by it, but he backspun it perfectly,” Rea said. “And then the right fielder almost caught it, too. It’s cool to watch moments like that.</p><p>“I turned it on in the eighth, so I turned it on at the perfect time.”</p><p>Rea is a baseball fan off the field, and watching games and highlights is part of his routine, especially when his children — ages 9, 7, 5 and 3 — are in town.</p><p>“As soon as we get home from the field, it’s turn the game on, and we watch all the highlights,” he said. “They love it.”</p><p>And Rea has a fondness for the Sox. He played with Sox manager Will Venable in 2015 with the Padres, he worked with Sox bench coach Walker McKinven with the Brewers and he’s good friends with Sox reliever Bryan Hudson, with whom he played in Milwaukee.</p><p>“I’m rooting for them,” Rea said.</p>

entries.title: Irving Park man suspected of carrying out string of Avondale sexual attacks charged
entries.summary: <p>Witnesses helped lead to the arrest of a Northwest Side man who allegedly attacked two women and a 16-year-old girl during three separate Avondale incidents Friday night that happened minutes apart, prosecutors said Wednesday.</p><p>Zayer Picado-Sevilla, 33, is charged with felony counts of aggravated criminal sexual abuse causing bodily harm and attempted aggravated criminal sexual assault causing bodily harm in connection with the attack of a 39-year-old woman, which happened at 8:05 p.m. in the 3300 block of North Springfield Avenue, prosecutors and police said.</p><p>At a detention hearing at Leighton Criminal Courthouse Wednesday, prosecutors said Picado-Sevilla is suspected in two similar abuses, including the assault of a 24-year-old woman at 8:18. p.m., just blocks from the Springfield attack, and the attack of a 16-year-old girl at about 8:50 p.m., about a half mile away from the initial assault.</p><p>Picado-Sevilla was also charged with driving with a never-issued license, a misdemeanor, and citations for obstructing a driver’s view and carrying alcohol as a driver, Chicago police said.</p><p>A judge Wednesday ordered Picado-Sevilla detained pending trial.</p><p>Investigators said a link in the cases was a red sedan that Picado-Sevilla was seen driving at the time of the attacks. A witness to the second attack saw Picado-Sevilla and took a photo of his license plate as he fled the scene.</p><p>Officers ran a FLOCK investigation based on the times of the three incidents and found the vehicle was registered in Picado-Sevilla's name to an address near the assault of the 16-year-old girl, prosecutors said.</p><p>Picado-Sevilla allegedly said he was “being chased” and was “drunk” during the alleged attacks, prosecutors said.</p><p>Prosecutors said the 39-year-old woman was on her nightly walk at about 8:05 p.m. when Picado-Sevilla stepped aside to let her pass before grabbing her. He allegedly groped her and tried to kiss her, prosecutors said. </p><p>Picado-Sevilla knocked the woman to the ground, but a man who heard her screams from a nearby CTA stop ran over, confronted Picado-Sevilla and briefly chased him, prosecutors said.</p><p>About 13 minutes later, prosecutors said, a 24-year-old woman walking home from a friend’s house was grabbed from behind as Picado-Sevilla forced his hand up her thigh. A neighbor heard the woman’s screams, ran from his apartment, and photographed the car’s license plate, prosecutors said.</p><p>About 22 minutes later, prosecutors said, a 16-year-old girl was walking home after stopping at an ice cream shop near her school when Picado-Sevilla grabbed her from behind, repeatedly struck her in the groin and dragged her toward his car.</p><p>The girl collapsed and covered herself, but Picado-Sevilla reportedly continued striking her while pulling her toward the vehicle, prosecutors said.</p><p>The girl escaped after Picado-Sevilla opened the car door as a passerby drove past, and Picado-Sevilla fled the scene, prosecutors said. The girl suffered abrasions and bruising and called her father.</p><p>After gathering data from FLOCK cameras, officers pulled Picado-Sevilla over on Monday for a traffic stop and detained him for driving with an open alcohol container and driving without a valid license.</p><p>Picado-Sevilla’s criminal background includes a 2024 Texas arrest for violating the Alien Inadmissibility Act. He also has pending investigations related to assaults on the 16-year-old girl and the 24-year-old woman, prosecutors said.</p><p>Picado-Sevilla is due back in court on Oct. 6.</p>

entries.title: Indiana man charged in armed robbery attempt at Orland Park gas station
entries.summary: <p>A 20-year-old Indiana man is facing charges after he allegedly attempted an armed robbery Tuesday morning at an Orland Park gas station.</p><p>Orland Park police responded at about 9 a.m. to reports of gunfire at a Shell gas station at 15100 Harlem Ave., village officials said in a statement.</p><p>Police said Christopher Brown, who was masked, approached a man pumping gas and pointed a gun at him while demanding his property.</p><p>The man, an Illinois concealed carry license holder, fired a gun and struck Brown once in the cheek, police said.</p><p>Brown fled the area and was found in a parking lot near 15100 73rd Ave., police said. He was taken by ambulance to a local hospital, where he was listed in stable condition, police said. The other man was not injured.</p><p>Police said the vehicle Brown drove and his weapon were reported stolen from Michigan City, Indiana.</p><p>Brown was charged by Cook County prosecutors with attempted armed robbery, possession of a stolen motor vehicle, possession of a stolen firearm, and two counts of aggravated unlawful possession of a weapon, police said.</p>

entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Alex Bregman make case that Cubs’ bats could bash their way through playoffs
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> believe they’re still <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/16/cubs-world-series-mlb-playoffs-nl-wild-card-standings-michael-conforto" >capable of winning the World Series</a>, even during a late-season downturn that’s seen them win only four of their last 10 series.</p><p>But even the doubters panicking over the team’s shaky bullpen had to be somewhat less skeptical watching the best bats in baseball bash the Braves in Wednesday night’s 8-4 win.</p><p>Center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong, miles ahead in the MVP race, kept adding to his untouchable resume, smacking two home runs to grow his season total to 44. He drove in three runs and tripled, now with more than 80 extra-base hits on the campaign.</p><p>“You’re shaking your head in amazement sometimes. In amazement,” manager Craig Counsell said. “You spend your whole life in baseball, and you just don’t see this happen on the baseball field. You’re grateful to be a part of it. You’re grateful to see things like this.</p><p>“And you’re grateful that the fans get to see a season like this, because they’re going to tell their kids about it, they’re going to tell their grandkids about seasons like this.”</p><p>As unbelievable as Crow-Armstrong has been, however, this is hardly some one-man operation, and third baseman Alex Bregman – whose bat has been electric in the second half after a slow start to his Cubs tenure – could find himself placing somewhere in the MVP vote, too.</p><p>Bregman, who started Wednesday sixth among NL position players in fWAR, came a single shy of hitting for the cycle – which Crow-Armstrong did earlier this season – banging out a trio of extra-base hits, including his 26th homer of the campaign. He drove in four runs.</p><p>Bregman slumped hard enough that he was getting booed at the supposedly Friendly Confines in the early going, but he’s been spectacular since the All-Star break, with a 1.034 OPS in his last 58 games.</p><p>The duo fell short of being just the second in team history to hit for the cycle in the same season; Billy Williams and Randy Hundley did it in 1966.</p><p>But they could find themselves doing something those 60s teams full of All Stars and Hall of Famers never did: carrying the Cubs deep into the postseason.</p><p>While the team’s pitching issues have been glaring enough to throw into question what it’s capable of come October, the Cubs still have the highest-scoring offense in baseball.</p><p>“It’s always fun to be a part of,” Crow-Armstrong said of a clicking lineup. “It definitely makes your life a little easier when you just know that someone can get the job done at any second.</p><p>“We’ve seen it time and time again, and when it is going like it is right now, it’s fun. It feels free and about as close to easy as baseball can get.”</p><p>Sure, neither Crow-Armstrong or Bregman pitch, and that’s where the question marks hang over the Cubs and their chances of reaching their season-long, championship-level goals.</p><p>But if they’re doing this to opposing pitching, will it matter?</p><p>“We’re swinging at good pitches right now. We’re damaging the pitches that we get,” Bregman said. “That’s what it’s going to take down the stretch.”</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams turns to simpler approach and gets spectacular results as more decisive passer
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams’ summer was all flashbulbs and viral videos, a pre-celebration of where the world believed he was headed.</p><p>Then he delivered on the hype with boring, fundamental play from the pocket.</p><p>That was what the Bears had been waiting for since they drafted him No. 1 overall in 2024. The off-the-charts talent has been there since college, but he lagged in the basics — until Sunday.</p><p>As the Bears’ offense <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/13/bears-inactives-vs-panthers-for-week-1-backup-qb-tyson-bagent-inactive-but-designated-as-emergency-3rd-qb" >torched the Panthers 59-37</a> to open the season, setting a franchise record for total yardage at 552, Williams seemed like a different quarterback compared to his first two seasons, and the clearest change was his decisiveness.</p><p>On every drop-back, he looked like he had a plan. He read and exploited defensive coverages. He knew all the answers to the test and moved through it quickly.</p><p>He smiled and said, “Second year in the offense,” when asked about that Wednesday after practice. And maybe it’s just that simple.</p><p>“I’m not necessarily thinking about the play,” Williams said. “The play is on my mind and I know where the guys are going to be, but it’s more [seeing] the coverage and... if they don’t give us the right coverage, find a checkdown, get the ball out of my hands.</p><p>“I’m not holding the ball too long. There’s going to be plays where I’m going to do that and go make a play, but just trying to minimize those.”</p><p>With that approach against the Panthers, he didn’t make many throws that were actually amazing. He didn’t need to. It was all about sound choices and cashing in on low-risk, high-reward opportunities — exactly what coach Ben Johnson has been teaching him for two years.</p><p>Williams’ 22-yard touchdown pass to tight end Cole Kmet stands as his most jaw-dropping throw — rolling right, turning left, launching the ball to the perfect spot for Kmet’s over-the-shoulder diving catch — and he made another impressive one to wide receiver Kalif Raymond for 28 yards later in the quarter while scrambling left.</p><p>But mostly, he took advantage of open receivers underneath and threw passes that led his teammates toward space. He completed 14 of 15 throws within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage. It was somewhat in the style of Drew Brees, especially late in his career with the Saints.</p><p>That’s no coincidence.</p><p>Brees, a recently inducted Hall of Famer who set the record for single-season completion percentage at 74.4 in 2018, was on Fox’s broadcast crew for the game and talked with Williams in a production meeting leading up to it.</p><p>Brees told Williams the difference between completing 60% of his passes and 70% was finding three more completions per game, and Johnson grinned as he said, “That might’ve stuck with our guy a little bit, which was cool to see,” before highlighting how proficiently Williams went through his reads and made timely checkdowns.</p><p>“He’s a legend... so when he says things like that, it moves you, especially when you watched him growing up,” Williams said of Brees.</p><p>He interpreted Brees’ advice as, “Know where the checkdowns are, but also [have] confidence in your guys,” then demonstrated both principles against the Panthers while completing 21 of 29 passes for 269 yards and two touchdowns with no turnovers for a 124.1 passer rating.</p><p>“When it's not there, just find the guy in front of you,” Williams said.</p><p>That’s what he’d been missing.</p><p>From the beginning, even amid the haphazard coaching he got as a rookie under Matt Eberflus and Shane Waldron, the Bears saw that he could do the exceptional but needed help with the essential. It was part of what drew them to Johnson.</p><p>The basis of an elite passing game is a lot of relatively easy yardage on passes underneath, then a few deep shots stacked on top of it. That’s the precise template Williams used Sunday.</p><p>"He continues to play with more anticipation and he understands what we're trying to get done,” Johnson said. “He played with a lot of confidence, and when you do that, you're seeing the field really well — he’s always done that — and the game slows down to a degree and he's able to get to the right guy a little bit faster than in the past. Hopefully that growth continues."</p><p>That’s the key. The Panthers game was a moment, and Williams has had those before. He lit up the Jaguars in London early in his rookie season, then he and the team plunged. He was up and down last season even after appearing to turn a corner. The way he played Sunday must go from novel to normal for him.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Chase bank shouldn't demolish its modernist Evanston branch
entries.summary: <p>Unless you have some business at the Chase bank at Green Bay Road and Central Street in Evanston, it's easy to pass through the busy intersection without ever really noticing the one-story building.</p><p>But the cool little brick-and-glass bank branch is worth a look — while it's still there.</p><p>JPMorgan Chase & Co wants to demolish the 47-year-old building and erect a new, smaller branch on the site.</p><p>Evanston's Historic Preservation Commission thinks the structure is valuable enough to at least consider landmarking. </p><p>The panel took up the issue at its meeting Tuesday but decided to postpone a vote for 60 days at the request of Chase, which objects to the building receiving landmark status.</p><p>Evanston resident James McKee, an architecture buff, had submitted a request to the town's planning officials suggesting they seek landmark status for the bank. His ask helped put the building before the preservation commission.</p><p>"I thought it was worthy of nominating for landmark status since Chase is planning to demolish it," McKee said. "You know, if we don't landmark it, they've got a plan in place ... to close it, demolish it, build a new branch. It would be a real shame to lose."</p><p>In a town chock-full of great architecture, would the demolition of a humble bank branch count as a loss? Indeed it would.</p><p>The pavilion-like brick-and-glass building was designed by the late David Haid, a very fine architect who lived in Evanston and studied under Mies van der Rohe at the Illinois Institute of Technology. And he worked in Mies's Chicago office before forming his own architecture firm.</p><p>Much of Haid's work bears a design kinship to Mies: minimalist, glassy, boxy and well-turned.</p><p>His best designs include Walter H. Dyett High School for the Arts, composed of two low-slung jet black beauties — an academic building and a natatorium — at 555 E. 51st St. in Washington Park and the architect's own Evanston residence.</p><p>"Haid is now widely regarded as a prominent master of steel-and-glass structural expression in his own right," Cade Sterling, preservation planner with Evanston's Office of Historic Preservation, said in a report to the commission. "His body of work actively extended from his Miesian foundation — representing one of the purest, most refined expressions of the Second Chicago School [of architecture] during the critical transitional era of Late Modernism."</p><p>But Haid's most recognized work is the black steel-and-glass residential auto pavilion in Highland Park, where Cameron Frye's dad kept that ill-fated red Ferrari in the 1986 movie "Ferris Bueller's Day Off." The architect supervised the repair of the pavilion's glass after the scene. </p><p>Haid died in 1993 at age 64.</p><p>Built in 1979 as the First National Bank and Trust of Evanston, Haid's Chase bank is a subtle and clever structure.</p><p>At its Central Street main entrance, the blonde brick building seems to part like a curtain to make way for a full-story glass entry. But at the Green Bay Road side, the brick pulls a vanishing act and the bank greets Green Bay with just a pure steel-and-glass wall.</p><p>And inside, the original single-room, column-free banking hall is largely intact. The ceiling is a remarkable exposed structural grid with lighted panels.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Inside the endangered Chase bank at 1900 Central St. in Evanston.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by James McKee</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"It's hard to make a simple building really beautiful, and I think [Haid] succeeds at that," said architectural historian Susan S. Benjamin who co-authored the book "Modern in the Middle: Chicago Houses 1929-75" with Michelangelo Sabatino.</p><p>"This is special," she said of the bank. "This is really special."</p><p>In a written objection to the preservation commission JPMorgan Chase & Co. Vice President Jonathan Krissoff said the building is "utilitarian" and not worthy of landmark status.</p><p>Haid "never pushed the boundaries or advanced the profession in the way that other of Mies’ students, employees or other modernist did, such as truly renowned architects Bertrand Goldberg, Harry Weese, Helmut Jahn, Phillip Johnson, Myron Goldsmith or Bruce Graham to name just a few," Krissoff wrote.</p><p>Krissoff and Chase should rethink their response.</p><p>JPMorgan Chase says it needs a smaller branch in the site. Fair enough.</p><p>But think of the blinding amount of resources that company holds. It has enough money to consider virtually any solution under the sun that could preserve and restore the building, while creating whatever new space the bank wants.</p><p>To simply send in demolition equipment to rip into the building and lay waste to that lovely banking hall is distasteful and an affront to good architecture.</p><p>They've got some time to reconsider. The commission will revisit the landmark recommendation on Nov. 18.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Daughter-in-law appears to have eyes on my husband's money
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband (80) and I (72) have been married 25 years. This is the second marriage for both of us. Until three years ago, I felt I had a wonderful relationship with his family, so it's hard to deal with what he's done to me and my relationships with them.</p><p>A new daughter-in-law, "Jean," who has a granddaughter, "Sophie," has fostered a secret relationship between my husband and this child, who is now 4. I was shocked when they came over on his birthday last year and Sophie was all over him, calling him grandpa, etc. It was apparent what had been going on. I felt humiliated at being excluded but said nothing, as I had been looking forward to getting to know the child. I believe Jean has her eyes on my husband's money. I suspect he used our joint checking account to buy a life insurance policy with this little girl as a beneficiary. I believe Jean thinks my husband (and I) should foot the bill for Sophie's college education.</p><p>Now my husband wants a divorce. We've had some rocky years due to his health, but this takes the cake. This DIL is greedy and brazen. My husband did not want his son to marry her in the first place, but she had a plan. I have done nothing wrong (though he accuses me of cheating), and it is heartbreaking that his family is ghosting me. How do you fight a liar? — <i>ILL IN ILLINOIS</i></p><p><b>DEAR ILL:</b> Dealing with a manipulator like Jean can be a nightmare. If you haven't consulted a divorce lawyer, do so now, and make sure the insurance policy is the first thing you mention. A lot of your story is Jean's word against yours, but if such a policy was created without your knowledge, your husband could be in big trouble. It may be of utmost interest to your attorney.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My oldest son, "Mitch," from a previous marriage, passed away six months ago. He had five children and two grandchildren. Admittedly, I hadn't been the most attentive grandparent over the years. I got along well with them, but I wasn't always around because I was raising my own family.</p><p>Since Mitch's death, I haven't heard a word from any of them. His kids are grown; the youngest is 24. Mitch's wife has made it known that I am not needed in their lives. She said she needs time and space. I'm respecting that, but I'm not happy that I don't get to see one of my great-grandsons. Should I force the issue and show up at her door one day? I don't want to alienate them, but it's becoming obvious that I'm out of their lives forever. These are sad times. I miss my son as much as they do, but they don't care about me. — <i>DOWN AND OUT IN INDIANA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DOWN AND OUT:</b> You mentioned that you "weren't the most attentive" grandparent over the years. Did this include forgetting them on birthdays, Christmas, graduations and so forth? If the answer lies between "maybe" and "yes," then it shouldn't be surprising that your grandchildren learned to do without you in their lives. Allow me to offer this suggestion: Rather than show up unannounced, it might be more effective to reach out to them individually.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: A law requires Illinois schools to teach Asian American history. Is it happening?
entries.summary: <p>In 2021, Illinois passed a <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinois.gov/news/release.html?releaseid=23548" target="_blank" ><u>law</u></a> requiring every public <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/publicacts/view/102-0044" target="_blank" ><u>elementary and high school</u></a> to teach a unit of Asian American and Pacific Islander history.</p><p>Five years later, many schools throughout the state have yet to fully implement the Teaching Equitable Asian American Community History Act.</p><p>The Illinois State Board of Education developed a <a class="Link" href="https://www.isbe.net/Documents/TEAACH-Act-Resource-Guide.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>resource guide</u></a> to help schools build out AAPI history curricula. State Rep. Jennifer Gong-Gershowitz, D-Glenview, says she’s proud of the progress that’s been made so far — but there’s still work to be done.</p><p>Some advocates say they were met with mixed results while doing outreach to schools.</p><p>“Roughly 25% of teachers and students in the state of Illinois have had some participation with the Asian American curricular resources that have been made available since the bill passed,” Gong-Gershowitz, a sponsor of the bill, told WBEZ.</p><p>In 2026, WBEZ talked to Chicago-area educators, students and lawmakers about the TEAACH Act to see how the law has taken shape in some local schools.</p><h3>What led to the TEAACH Act?</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Jennifer Gong-Gershowitz and state Sen. Ram Villivalam watch Gov. J.B. Pritzker sign legislation that will require public school students to learn about Asian American history, July 8, 2021.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gong-Gershowitz said the momentum for the bill was prompted largely by <a class="Link" href="https://www.ajc.com/news/breaking-multiple-shootings-shut-down-busy-woodstock-highway/OLE23RVIO5BE3ELWBZAA6GVSSA/" target="_blank" ><u>high-profile cases</u></a> of anti-Asian hate crimes during the COVID-19 pandemic. She presented the bill <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=376&GAID=16&GA=102&DocTypeID=HB&LegID=128327&SessionID=110" target="_blank" ><u>in committee</u></a> the day after a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chds.us/c/timeline/atlanta-spa-shootings/" target="_blank" ><u>mass shooting</u></a> in March at several Atlanta-area spas killed eight people, including six Asian women.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoissenatedemocrats.com/caucus-news/46-senator-ram-villivalam-news/2760-governor-signs-historic-asian-american-curriculum-bill-into-law" target="_blank" ><u>coalition of more than 35 organizations</u></a>, including Asian Americans Advancing Justice Chicago, championed the bill — the first of its kind anywhere in the United States.</p><p>Some of the bill’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2021/05/24/illinois-bill-aims-to-ensure-asian-american-experiences-arent-ignored-in-history-class" target="_blank" ><u>opponents said</u></a> decisions about curricula should happen at the local level, rather than being mandated by the state.</p><p>The bill ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://glas.uic.edu/news-stories/victory-teaach-act-passed-108-10/" target="_blank" ><u>passed</u> t</a>he Illinois State House <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Documents/legislation/votehistory/102/house/10200HB0376sam002_05312021_015000C.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>108-10</u></a> on May 31, 2021. A committee of local educators worked together to organize resources and standardize a curriculum.</p><p>The TEAACH Act was unfunded when it first passed, but in 2025, Illinois committed <a class="Link" href="http://google.com/url?q=https://advancingjustice-chicago.org/llinois-commits-2-million-to-inclusive-history-education/&sa=D&source=docs&ust=1789163171685341&usg=AOvVaw1w97-t3rsxtKix_plVi-_g" target="_blank" ><u>$2 million</u></a> to inclusive K-12 history mandates. Some of that money was allocated to meeting the TEAACH Act’s mandate. It found 73% of student respondents say they received “little to no” education focusing on Asian American communities during the previous school year.</p><p>Some educators have seen those percentages play out in the classroom.</p><p>John Lee teaches an Asian American Studies elective at Niles West High School in Skokie. He estimates he instructs up to about 13% of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoisreportcard.com/school.aspx?source=studentcharacteristics&source2=enrollmentbygrades&Schoolid=050162190170003" target="_blank" ><u>senior class</u></a>.</p><p>Lee says about half of his students haven’t heard about fundamental moments from Asian American history in his curriculum before starting his class. It includes historical events like the <a class="Link" href="https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/chinese-exclusion-act" target="_blank" ><u>Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882</u></a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://history.house.gov/Historical-Highlights/1951-2000/Immigration-and-Nationality-Act-of-1965/" target="_blank" ><u>Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965</u></a>. Niles West didn’t respond to Lee’s comments when asked. The festival, which featured cultural performances, small businesses, food, and arts and crafts, aims to celebrate Asian, South Asian and Pacific Islander art and culture and raise awareness to prevent anti-Asian violence, according to their website.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Some states have established AAPI requirements through a patchwork of different laws and standards.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://california100.org/ethnic-studies-for-all-californias-new-high-school-requirement/" target="_blank" ><u>California law</u></a> signed in 2021 requires all high schools in the state to offer an ethnic studies course. The act went into effect the <a class="Link" href="https://pub.njleg.gov/bills/2020/S4500/4021_I1.HTM" target="_blank" ><u>2022–2023</u></a> school year. The mandate was also unfunded when it passed.</p><h3>What do students say about Asian American history courses?</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d30000" name="image-d30000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d97bac5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fae%2F5d%2F12d3e8ea4f58b1b5d1addd3e3740%2Fteaachactaniversary-260817-17.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b24434/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fae%2F5d%2F12d3e8ea4f58b1b5d1addd3e3740%2Fteaachactaniversary-260817-17.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f63a712/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fae%2F5d%2F12d3e8ea4f58b1b5d1addd3e3740%2Fteaachactaniversary-260817-17.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Alexa John and Isha George give a presentation on the SAVE Act to fellow high school students at the HANA Center - Northwest Center located at 664 N. The group is pushing the districts to fully implement the TEAACH Act. That <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/Da3B0yzjcjt/?img_index=4" target="_blank" ><u>includes</u></a> ensuring accomplishments by Asian American people are included in history curricula and including at least two pieces of Asian American literature in English courses.</p><p>Ahir Naveen, a junior at John Hersey High School in Arlington Heights, is working to collect student signatures in support of their demands and return to leadership with the petition.</p><p>“I think that with knowledge comes power, and with knowledge comes understanding of other people and perspectives broadening,” Naveen said.</p>

entries.title: In Little Village, a year after Midway Blitz, some vow to stay, others worry they can't afford to
entries.summary: <p>Little Village faced displacement and gentrification pressures long before Operation Midway Blitz. It’s part of South Lawndale, where in 2024, nearly half of renters were spending more than 30% of their income on housing. The neighborhood’s proximity to downtown and rapidly gentrifying Pilsen–Little Village's boundaries are roughly from Cermak to 31st Street, and from Sacramento to Kostner–had also fueled concerns that development could push longtime residents and businesses out.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-a00000" name="html-embed-module-a00000"></a><div style="min-height:496px" id="datawrapper-vis-R3VIB"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/R3VIB/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-R3VIB"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/R3VIB/full.png" alt="A map of central Chicago. The northeast corner is roughly where the east-to-west branch of the Chicago River meets Lake Michigan, and the southwest corner is near the intersection of 31st Street and Kostner Avenue, close to the Target and Portillo’s stores in Cicero. Three areas are highlighted in green. The first highlighted area, taking up roughly one-third of the horizontal span of the map and roughly one-quarter of its vertical span, is all the way in the bottom left corner (southwest). It is shown in a darker green than the others, and it has a large, bold label that says “Little Village”. The second highlighted area, near the center of the map, is a bit narrower vertically, so it stretches more lengthwise from west to east. It is shown in a light green, and it has a more muted label that says “Pilsen”. The third highlighted area is the smallest of the three and is located at the top right corner (northeast) of the map. It has the same light green color and muted label style as Pilsen does, and its label says “Loop”. An inset map of the Chicago city limits in the top left (northwest) of the map shows this is pretty close to the center of the city, perhaps just north of the same. 26th Street is drawn and labeled on the map and cuts directly through the middle of Little Village from west to east. The CTA Pink Line also appears; it starts off the western edge of the map, travels east, passes just north of Little Village itself, turns northward near the middle of Pilsen, and turns east again near the northern edge of the map and continues to the Loop itself. Other north-to-south streets labeled for clarity are, from left to right: Kostner Avenue, Pulaski Road, Kedzie Avenue and California Avenue. Little Village itself stretches from Kostner on the west to somewhere between Kedzie and California on the east. Pulaski is about one-third of the way across the neighborhood if starting from Kostner." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The COVID-19 pandemic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/2/16/22280624/chicago-latino-businesses-covid-covid19-coronavirus-pandemic-economy" target="_blank" ><u>brought another period of upheaval</u></a>, forcing some businesses to close and leaving others struggling.</p><p>Then came President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.</p><p>During the height of Operation Midway Blitz, federal immigration agents detained 3,841 people, according to federal data analyzed by the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ.</p><p>Little Village became one of the most visible targets. Federal agents made arrests in the neighborhood on the first full day of Midway Blitz and returned repeatedly in the months that followed.</p><p>On Oct. 22 and 23 and again on Nov. 8, large groups of federal agents descended on Little Village, carrying out arrests and confronting residents and protesters. The <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/inv-briefs/IAC-Little-Village-Investigation-Brief-r.pdf" target="_blank" >Illinois Accountability Commission</a> later singled out those three days for an investigation of what it described as an “occupation” of the neighborhood.</p><p>The effects extended beyond the arrests. Fear of immigration agents kept people home. Shops and restaurants emptied, battering Little Village’s commercial corridors. <a class="Link" href="https://greatcities.uic.edu/news-stories/hunkering-down-the-hidden-economic-cost-of-federal-immigration-enforcement-in-cook-county-il/" target="_blank" ><u>A University of Illinois Chicago analysis</u></a> released this month estimated that increased immigration enforcement that started in January of 2025 resulted in $1.26 billion in lost retail and restaurant activity across Cook County over the course of the following year. Researchers said residents of neighborhoods with large numbers of “Latin America-born” people made fewer trips to stores and restaurants outside their communities, a dip that continued for nearly a year.</p><p>Immigration enforcement is quieter and less visible now, but the Trump administration continues to arrest hundreds of people each month.</p><p>In Little Village, many continue to stay home, and some business owners are spending money accumulated over generations to remain open. Some are questioning whether they can afford to stay there.</p><p>The Sun-Times spoke with residents, business owners and a neighborhood realtor about how immigration enforcement is reshaping Little Village—straining businesses, prompting property offers and leading some residents to invest in Mexico as they reconsider their futures in Chicago.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>She fought displacement. Now she is wondering whether she can stay</h3><p>María de la Luz Rodríguez, 61, who’s lived in Little Village for 19 years,<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/9/15/23860232/gentrification-little-village-housing-coop-tenants-rent-real-estate-cooperative" > started working</a> with the housing cooperative <a class="Link" href="https://www.lavillitahousingcoop.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Cooperativa La Villita</u></a> after watching apartment buildings change hands and tenants get pushed out. Rodríguez, from Veracruz, Mexico, helped develop and write the cooperative’s bylaws in Spanish and English, handed out flyers and spoke at community meetings<i>. </i>Eventually, the cooperative purchased its first building, a six-unit property on Whipple Street. According to its website, estimated monthly housing charges range from $950 to $1,150. By this summer, Rodríguez says, all of its apartments were occupied and the group was working toward buying another.</p><p>“The cooperative is a group of people who really love Little Village,” Rodríguez says in Spanish.</p><p>But Rodríguez, who does not have legal status, says her own ability to remain in Little Village has become uncertain. She lost her retail job after her employer began using the federal system E-Verify to check whether staffers are authorized to work in the United States.</p><p>She planned to purchase a cooperative membership but could not afford to after she became unemployed. She continues to volunteer as a board member.</p><p>She also lost work as a community health promoter after funding dried up. Now she is struggling to cover her rent.</p><p>Peddling has become one way to get by. <a class="Link" href="https://streetvendorsac.org/" target="_blank" ><u>The Street Vendors Association of Chicago</u></a> gave her $500 in assistance. She packs buñuelos and Veracruz-style peanuts into a suitcase and takes her wares to community and health fairs because there is more foot traffic than the Little Village business corridor.</p><p>“Little Village is dead,” she says.</p><p>Rodríguez says people in Little Village do not want to leave. Neighbors watch out for one another.</p><p>She is nevertheless considering leaving herself.</p><p>Rodríguez has family in Mexico and is thinking about returning to Veracruz. “There may not be much money there,” she says, “But at least I can have a coffee outside in my garden, or go outside for a walk and they are not going to grab me.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div homeowners in Little Village for years. The RE/MAX broker says families there tend to hold onto their properties for decades, resulting in relatively little turnover.</p><p>But Villegas is seeing some immigrant families consider a different future.</p><p>Villegas says she has worked with several Little Village clients who have invested in property in Mexico, including families who are looking for a possible place to live in the future. The developers she works with are primarily in larger Mexican cities, while she believes Little Village families who actually return to Mexico may be more likely to go back to their hometowns.</p><p>There are other signs that more Chicago-area families are keeping Mexico within reach. Requests at the Mexican Consulate in Chicago to register U.S.-born people for Mexican nationality more than doubled, from 3,800 in 2024 to 9,646 in 2025, according to the consulate.</p><p>Through Villegas’ network, land can start at about $35,000, condos at $100,000 and homes at $135,000.</p><p>“You don’t know what the future looks like because of the current policy, and what it will continue to do to families long term,” she says.</p><p>Villegas has built a network of contacts in Mexico who can help clients find housing, start businesses and make a living. For families considering leaving the United States, she says, her job is not simply to sell their home but to help them figure out what comes next.</p><p>“What is the plan,” she says, “and how can we get you to that plan?”</p><p>Villegas says someone who has paid off a home over decades may be able to buy a house for substantially less in parts of Mexico and live on what remains.</p><p>But she has encountered homeowners prepared to accept unsolicited offers before realizing they could be giving up $50,000, $60,000 or $70,000 in equity.</p><p>The decision to buy in Mexico is rarely about one thing, she says. An owner may be dealing with problems involving tenants, building repair costs or a business that is struggling. Immigration status can make navigating those problems even harder.</p><p>Eventually, Villegas says, the pressures can accumulate.</p><p>“Sometimes people just are also tired,” she says. “Sometimes people don’t have the will to fight anymore.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-540000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chef and owner José Luis López stands behind the counter with his wife Clarita at Los Candiles Restaurant in Little Village.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Going where the customers are </b></h3><p>Around 1 p.m. on Aug. 13, Los Candiles restaurant at 2624 S. Central Ave. was nearly empty.</p><p>José Luis (Louie) López was there with a kitchen worker and his wife, Clarita López, 40, who waits tables. There were plenty of tables but few customers.</p><p>López, 44, pulled out the paper calendars he keeps to record the number of kitchen orders the restaurant fills each day. Before the pandemic, the restaurant typically recorded 40 to 50 kitchen orders on weekdays. Saturdays could bring as many as 90. Sundays, helped by church traffic, could reach 110.</p><p>He pointed to this year’s calendar. One Tuesday had 12 orders. Another day had 14. Saturdays that once reached 90 were now in the 30s.</p><p>“Everything is at half,” López says.</p><p>His parents opened Los Candiles in 1995. The family owns the building and finished paying it off about a decade ago. That has spared López a rent or mortgage payment as business has fallen.</p><p>But owning the building has not brought customers through the door.</p><p>López says immigration enforcement is only part of what has hurt the restaurant. Food costs have risen and customers have less money to spend. When rumors spread that immigration agents have returned, he says, people become frightened again.</p><p>To cope, he has increasingly taken Los Candiles outside Little Village.</p><p>López began offering <i>taquizas</i>, or catered taco parties, in 2017. He brings a flat-top grill, rice and beans, tortillas and trays of toppings and cooks for customers on site.</p><p>“That’s what’s keeping our head above water,” Lopez says.</p><p>He approached Cody’s Public House, a bar in Lakeview with an idea for selling tacos there on Thursdays. The relationship eventually became a weekly gig.</p><p>López says Los Candiles can sell more tacos during four hours at Cody’s than during seven hours at the restaurant in Little Village.</p><p>“We made double the tips.”</p><p>Without catering and the <i>taquizas</i>, López says, “We would have been long gone.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" stops moving. The president of the Little Village Community Council zips from one conversation to another with the people seeking advice and help at his office. School supplies and diapers are on hand for people in need. When immigration agents began operating heavily in Little Village last fall, he became one of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2025/12/02/as-immigration-agents-swept-chicago-this-fall-communities-stepped-in-to-get-kids-to-school-safely" target="_blank" ><u>neighborhood’s most visible organizers</u></a>, warning residents about reported ICE sightings and helping coordinate community response. He also owns a five-unit building in the 2300 block of South Trumbull Ave.</p><p>Unsolicited real estate inquiries about his property are not new. Enriquez says they began picking up during the COVID-19 pandemic. But since Midway Blitz’s last fall they have become much more frequent.</p><p>“I get mail, phone calls, emails,” Enriquez says. On some days, Enriquez estimates he receives as many as 30 solicitations. Some ask whether he wants to sell. Others offer financing. He has saved screenshots of text messages from people asking about his property, as well as a late-August mailer from Sherman Property, a cash home-buying business, designed to look like a check made out to him for $316,222.</p><p>He says prospective buyers have offered as much as $1 million to purchase his building. He has refused.</p><p>One of his tenants, a senior who has lived in the building for 15 years, still pays $800 a month for a three-bedroom apartment. Enriquez says the man has told him that if the rent went up, he would have to leave and start over somewhere else, away from the doctors and neighborhood he knows. He says a new owner could charge $1,300 or $1,500 for the same unit.</p><p>Little Village businesses are still recovering from months when customers stayed home amid immigration enforcement. Property owners are dealing with higher taxes and the costs of maintaining aging buildings.The ICE operations, he believes, made things worse.</p><p>“They put [in] more fuel,” he says.</p><p>Enriquez has spent years trying to build a life, investments and a future in Little Village. The question, he says, is whether everyone else will have the same choice.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3> <b>The cost of staying</b> </h3><p>Around 4 p.m. on Aug. 13 Osito’s Tap was quiet and dimly lit. A bartender arranged liquor bottles as Mike Moreno Jr., 35, settled into a table nearby. The first customers had yet to arrive.</p><p>Moreno’s family has been doing business in Little Village for more than half a century. His grandfather operated grocery stores in the neighborhood and his father opened Moreno’s Liquors on 26th Street in 1977. Moreno later opened Osito’s Tap near 26th and Ridgeway.</p><p>The family has survived difficult times before, including the COVID-19 pandemic. But Moreno says immigration enforcement operations brought another kind of strain.</p><p>From August through November last year, business at Osito’s and Moreno’s Liquors fell by half for two months and by at least 25% during the other two, Moreno says. The family cut costs and expanded delivery. They avoided layoffs.</p><p>They also began spending savings.</p><p>“We’re literally taking it from generations and generations, years and years of wealth that we built, and just reinvesting it and popping it back into our own businesses,” Moreno says.</p><p>Moreno’s family owns properties in Little Village and has no intention of selling. But he says the inquiries from speculators have become increasingly difficult to ignore.</p><p>Before the ICE arrests, Moreno says, he might receive four or five calls a week from people interested in buying property or offering financing. Now, he sometimes gets four or five in a day.</p><p>Moreno says one caller told him he had seen media reports about the raids and their economic impact on Little Village businesses before asking about Moreno’s property.</p><p>He usually blocks the numbers.</p><p>“We’re not selling,” Moreno says. “We’ve been here for almost 50 years, and we’ll be here for another 50.”</p><p>“As long as we work really hard,” Moreno says, “we can keep what’s ours.”</p>

entries.title: 'Starved Rock killer' died last year, but his family is now seeking a rare posthumous pardon from Pritzker
entries.summary: <p>The decades-long fight to clear Chester Weger’s name as the notorious "Starved Rock Killer" isn’t ending with his death.</p><p>Weger’s family will get a chance next month to argue that the man who spent nearly six decades behind bars was wrongly convicted in one of Illinois’ most infamous murder cases.</p><p>The Illinois Prisoner Review Board has scheduled a rare Oct. 6 hearing in Chicago on the family’s request for a posthumous pardon from Gov. JB Pritzker.</p><p>The board rarely has considered posthumous clemency petitions, holding such hearings for only two other people in the past seven years.</p><p>Weger was sentenced to life in prison in 1961 for killing one of the three women whose battered bodies were found near a cave at Starved Rock State Park, a popular getaway spot for Chicagoans.</p><p>He confessed to the killings but quickly recanted — then spent the rest of his life insisting he was innocent.</p><p>Weger was paroled in 2020 for good behavior in prison after spending about 60 years behind bars, but his conviction remained on his record.</p><p>After his release, his lawyers launched a fresh effort to overturn the conviction, citing DNA evidence, new witness testimony and alternative theories about who killed Mildred Linquist, 50, Lillian Oetting, 50, and Frances Murphy, 47. They had gone to Starved Rock to hike and bird watch in March 1960.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a convicted.</p><p>Krajcir admitted to killing nine women and is serving an 80-year Illinois prison sentence.</p><p>Thompson’s nephew, the Illinois Innocence Project and police officer Paul Echols — who obtained Krajcir’s confession — pushed to clear Thompson’s name. </p><p>Then-Gov. Bruce Rauner granted Thompson a pardon in 2019.</p><p>The other recent case involves Joe James, a Black man executed in 1908 for killing a white man, Clergy Ballard, in Springfield.</p><p>Northwestern University’s Center on Wrongful Convictions and other advocates have argued James did not receive a fair trial. </p><p>An all-white jury convicted him just weeks after a white mob lynched two Black men and torched hundreds of Black homes and businesses during the Springfield race riot.</p><p>The Prisoner Review Board has sent Pritzker a confidential recommendation in James' case, and the governor has yet to act on it, according to a board spokesperson.</p>

entries.title: Chicago International Film Fest 2026 lineup announced
entries.summary: <p>In less than a month, about 45,000 cinephiles will descend on local theaters for the 62nd Chicago International Film Festival, which released its full lineup of 113 feature films and 57 shorts on Thursday.</p><p>The festival will open on Oct. 14 with a screening of Jordan Firstman’s acclaimed debut feature film, “Club Kid” (A24). It will close on Oct. 25 with Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” (Searchlight Pictures), starring Pedro Pascal and a “brilliantly unhinged” Olivia Wilde, according to Mimi Plauché, the event's artistic </div> </div><p>In fact, people under 35 have become the festival's largest demographic, accounting for more than 40% of its attendees, Plauché said. The shift is due in part to the inclusion of younger festival programmers, and the Letterboxd craze among movie-lovers who want to be the first to post reviews online, she said. But, most of all, audiences are looking for community.</p><p>“It’s very different to watch a comedy at home alone than with an audience of everybody who's laughing,” Plauché said. “We all feel differently when we're together. And we want to emphasize that we have films that not only make you see the world differently, but also make you feel differently about the world.”</p><p>The slate of films are directed by veterans and up-and-comers from more than 60 countries. Audiences can watch everything from Oscar contenders (“Wild Horse Nine”) and timely documentaries (the unsanctioned “Musk,” about Elon Musk) to gripping foreign dramas (“Fatherland” and “Sad Girlz”).</p><p>The fest will also program Chicago stories. Among the local tales are “No Hands: The Wild Ride of the Schwinn Bicycle Company” and the “Ever After” profile of Chef Curtis Duffy. “Mouse,” a film by Chicago-based directors Kelly O’Sullivan and entries.title: A new PBS documentary shows the intensity and heart behind the Joffrey Ballet's ‘Winning Works’ competition
entries.summary: <p>A new documentary captures the discipline, creativity and heart behind the Joffrey Ballet’s trailblazing “Winning Works” program for emerging artists <br>historically excluded from ballet.</p><p>“<a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/show/joffrey-ballet-the-next-movement/" target="_blank" >Joffrey Ballet: The Next Movement</a>” premieres Friday at 9 p.m. Eastern (8 p.m. Central) on PBS, <a class="Link" href="http://pbs.org" target="_blank" ><u>PBS.org</u></a> and the PBS app. The film was produced by Chicago-based Kartemquin Films and directed by South Sider Cam Be. It follows five choreographers over two weeks as they prepare new works featuring students from Joffrey’s Grainger Academy.</p><p>The piece not only highlights the intensity of staging performances, but the personal stories of the BIPOC artists, many of whom have had to pave their own way in an art form that has, until recent years, mostly featured white dancers and choreographers.</p><p>“I want you to understand the level of dedication it takes and the work these choreographers went through to get to the spaces they’re in,” said Cam Be, 44, of Bronzeville.</p><p>“But also, I want you to understand that they’re just human beings, and that they have life experiences and trauma that they’ve had to deal with, and they continue to push through.”</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Alsip Mayor John Ryan helped establish term limits in his town. Now that they affect him, will they be eased?
entries.summary: <p>A decade ago while a trustee on the Alsip village board, John Ryan led the charge to impose term limits on the mayor and other elected officials in the south suburb so nobody would be able to serve more than three consecutive four-year terms.</p><p>He marshaled enough support on the village board to get a binding referendum placed on the 2016 ballot, letting Alsip voters decide whether to impose those limits, which they did.</p><p>Today, Ryan is Alsip’s mayor and in the midst of his third consecutive term — but it may not be his last, after all.</p><p>That’s because his colleagues on the village board — with what the village clerk says was Ryan's support — recently decided to place a new referendum on the ballot in November that, if passed by Alsip voters, would extend term limits to four consecutive four-year terms.</p><p>That would provide an obvious benefit for Ryan should the ballot question pass, and should he run again and win. He’d not only stay in power longer, he would continue to get paid by taxpayers and accrue more service credits that would boost his public sector pension.</p><p>Among those to find an irony in the situation is Patrick Kitching, who was Alsip’s mayor at the time Ryan pushed for the 2016 referendum.</p><p>Calling his successor "no good," Kitching described this as another opportunistic policy reversal by Ryan, like when he pushed for a cut in the mayor’s salary while Kitching was in office and later, when Ryan took over, wanted a mayoral pay hike.</p><p>A bitter political rival of Ryan, Kitching fought the initial term limit, arguing he was a full-time mayor and while limits at the federal and state levels make sense, they could prohibit someone at the local level from growing into and becoming better at the job.</p><p>“Show me a town that has a full-time mayor and has term limits,” he said then, according to a Daily Southtown article. “Three terms for a mayor is ridiculous. We are all subject to term limits — it’s called voting.”</p><p>But Ryan argued at the time, according to the news story: “The mayor made every attempt to obstruct voters’ rights. Just let the voters decide.”</p><p>The village board approved that ballot question, Kitching vetoed it and the village board then overrode the veto.</p><p>Of the 4,716 people who ended up voting on the 2016 referendum, 3,832 supported the limits, or more than 80%, according to election records.</p><h3>Read Alsip’s new resolution, ballot question</h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/69/1f/cc7ac1f24944b458b3c4556ed42b/alsip-resolution.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>In August, the Alsip village board approved a resolution to place the question about changing the term limits on the Nov. 3 ballot.</p><p>The resolution includes wording similar to Kitching’s long-ago argument, saying “the Mayor and Board of Trustees recognize that maintaining experienced leadership while continuously encouraging qualified public service ensures efficient and stable municipal management.”</p><p>Asked about the new effort, Ryan told the Chicago Sun-Times via email: “We are not trying to undo term limits. The Alsip Village Board approved a resolution to place a question on the November 3, 2026, ballot, asking Alsip voters whether they wish to modify the consecutive term limits for the mayor, clerk and trustees from three terms to four.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ca0000" Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ryan didn’t respond to further questions, including his feelings on the proposed change to the term limits. He didn’t have to vote on the matter at the August meeting, but he registered no objection and publicly said it needed to be approved that night to meet the deadline for the ballot.</p><p>He won’t say whether he plans to run for reelection as his current term expires in 2029.</p><p>The existing term limits, when approved in 2016, were not applied retroactively, so even though Kitching was in the midst of his third term at the time, the restrictions went in place after the 2017 election. That means he would’ve been allowed to serve out three more consecutive terms if he won the corresponding elections.</p><p>But Kitching opted not to run again.</p><p>Instead, Ryan ran for mayor in 2017 and won by 60 votes against another opponent.</p><p>Ryan has been mayor of the community of just under 20,000 people ever since, most recently winning in the 2025 election while running unopposed.</p><p>Alsip Village Clerk Renee Harding says of the new term limit measure: “If this passes” as a referendum, Ryan “would be allowed to run for one more term” of four years, “not an additional 3 terms.”</p><p>Harding says Ryan “supports putting it on the ballot and hopes it passes so he can run for another term."</p><p>Other suburbs with term limits include Tinley Park and Skokie.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2020/10/2/21496244/alsip-mayor-john-ryan-salary" target="_blank" >To get elected, Alsip Mayor John Ryan bragged of cutting predecessor’s pay. Three years later, he wants a big raise.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/28/23810213/alsip-safespeed-red-light-camera-federal-investigation-subpoenas" target="_blank" >In Alsip red-light camera investigation, feds have done new interviews, issued subpoenas</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/11/1/20943920/michael-madigan-son-andrew-alsip-mayor-john-ryan-campaign-michael-del-galdo" target="_blank" >Speaker Madigan’s son got Alsip business, hit up mayor for campaign cash for his dad</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2019/10/7/20903665/we-dont-pay-people-off-ceo-red-light-camera-company-plays-defense-amid-probe" target="_blank" >‘We don’t pay people off,’ CEO of red-light camera company insists amid federal investigation</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

Nope, even though he gained the title “music director designate” almost two and a half years ago, it’s still one more season until they cross out that last word. Starting next season, he will be in town 10 subscription weeks a year, but this season it’s just five, three of which are stacked together this fall. Mäkelä’s first program features fellow Finn Jean Sibelius’s Symphony No. 7, a composer whose work Mäkelä has championed. Second is a CSO specialty, Gustav Mahler’s Symphony No. 9. And third, the rarely performed oratorio “Belshazzar’s Feast,” by 20th-century British composer William Walton, brings in the Symphony Chorus to kick things up the extra notch of poshness for the CSO’s gala, Symphony Ball. Adams St., Suite 350A<br><b>When</b>: Sept. 30</p><p>For 20 years, the JACK Quartet has been at the forefront of the avant-garde classical string quartet repertoire. In those two decades, they have undergone personnel changes, such that the quartet’s name no longer represents the first initials of its members (JACJ doesn’t have the same ring to it), but they soldier on performing outer-space new music that isn’t for everyone, including a few pieces from past tours performed in utter darkness. On this visit, they world-premiere a piece called “Dahlia,” written by the Princeton composer Juri Seo. They also bookend the program with two quartets by Turkish composer Cenk Ergün that work outside Western music’s standard equal-tempered tuning system, and play a piece by one of their violinists (and former Chicagoan) Austin Wulliman. Woodlawn Ave.<br><b>When</b>: Oct. 2</p><p>Choral singing requires more versatility of the voice than casual observers sometimes appreciate. Sometimes the singer needs to produce an unobtrusive, background timbre, other times one that cuts through the ensemble to highlight a solo line. To be great at it, a singer must have a flexible instrument and high-level listening skills, and the humility to participate as an equal member of an ensemble. The British vocal octet Voces8, if you’ve never heard them before, excels at every subtlety that exists in choral music, running the repertoire gamut from early music to the choral explosion of the past few decades. As is indicated by the huge streaming numbers on their well-produced videos, the choir-loving public has reached a consensus: Voces8 is probably the best chamber choir in the world today. <i>Tickets early 19th century and brought to South Carolina.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Leah Wellman</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.lyricopera.org/shows/upcoming/2026-27/Omar/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Omar</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where</b>: Lyric Opera of Chicago, 20 N. Wacker Dr.<br><b>When</b>: Oct. 23–28</p><p>The push to mount contemporary, English-language operas at Lyric Opera of Chicago has brought some powerful, vital music to their prominent stage, such as “Dead Man Walking,” “El último sueño de Frida y Diego” and “Fire Shut Up in My Bones.” This season, the company delivers “Omar,” based on the true story of Omar ibn Said, a scholar of Islam in West Africa who was kidnapped by slavers in the early 19th century and brought to South Carolina. The creators of the opera are Michael Abels, whose scores for Jordan Peele’s movies have garnered accolades, and Rhiannon Giddens, a MacArthur genius whose resume exceeds the space allotted to this blurb, so suffice it to say she knows a lot about American roots music and how to play it on all the instruments (including her voice). Lyric is giving this show the criminally low number of three performances, so booking is a sooner-rather-than-later situation. <i>Tickets from $70.</i></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://cso.org/concerts-tickets/on-stage/chicago-symphony-orchestra/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Nikolaj Szeps-Znaider’s residency</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where</b>:<b> </b>Chicago Symphony Orchestra, 220 S. Michigan Ave.<br><b>When</b>: Oct. 22–31</p><p>The Danish conductor Nikolaj Szeps-Znaider has such a good rapport with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra that they invited him for a two-week stay. The first program’s centerpiece is the Dvořák Cello Concerto with soloist Jian Wang, a terrific piece played by a terrific soloist, more than just a consolation prize if you missed out on Yo-Yo Ma tickets. The second program offers Brahms’ “Ein Deutsches Requiem,” in a thoughtful placement in the calendar near the Day of the Dead. Brahms began composing the piece soon after the death of his mother, eschewing the liturgical requiem texts and instead selecting biblical passages to provide consolation to the living, a gesture akin to the building of an ofrenda with objects particular to a beloved who has passed away. The fifth movement, which includes the text “I will comfort you, as a mother comforts,” is heartbreaking. <i>Tickets from $45.</i></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.baroque.org/Seasons/2026-2027/bach-s-mass-in-b-minor" target="_blank" ><b><u>Mass in B Minor</u></b></a></h3><p><b>Where</b>: Multiple locations<br><b>When</b>: Nov. 22–23</p><p>If you polled classical music aficionados on the unanswerable question of what’s on their shortlist for the greatest single piece of all time, you’d hear a lot of Beethoven 9, some Ring cycles and a lot of votes for Music of the Baroque’s November offering: Johann Sebastian Bach’s Mass in B Minor. It’s the biggest work of contrapuntal architecture from the composer who influenced the direction of Western music more than any other. The MoB orchestra and chorus amass their formidable forces, under the baton of the estimable Jane Glover, for the two-hour-plus piece, from the keening Kyrie at the opening, through the bubbly Gloria, the agonized Crucifixus, the solemn Sanctus and ending with the uplifting Dona Nobis Pacem. The quartet of vocal soloists includes the sensitive British baritone Roderick Williams and the nightingale-voiced soprano Joélle Harvey.<i>Tickets from $36.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d70000" name="module-d70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><b>Your guide to fall culture in Chicago </b></h3><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-f6c56c02-ac5f-11f1-988e-bd5e5ce8e98f"><li>The next big thing is happening on Chicago’s small stages. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/things-to-do/2026/09/04/theater-to-see-chicago-fall-storefront-tickets-new-plays-musicals" target="_blank" ><u>Here are 10 plays and musicals</u></a> not to miss this theater season.</li><li>The ultimate guide to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/movies-tv/2026/09/10/chicago-fall-film-festivals-events-things-to-do-movies-ciff-cuff-reeling" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago’s fall film festivals</u></a>, from Oscar contenders to local standouts</li><li>Evanston’s $32 million <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/03/evanston-northlight-theater-chicago-suburbs-arts-annex" target="_blank" ><u>new Northlight Theatre</u></a> wasn’t built for big crowds. It’s built for new plays.</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2026/09/08/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism-art-institute-chicago-paintings-impressionist-mural-worlds-fair-1893" target="_blank" ><u>“Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism”</u></a> is the Art Institute’s first deep-dive into Cassatt in more than 25 years and explores some of her historical Chicago ties.</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: 5 public universities in Illinois use controversial Flock cameras to surveil campus, records show
entries.summary: <p>As towns, cities and colleges in Illinois and across the country cut ties with Flock Safety, a <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/19/43/adaa6cdf4158a9edcceeef346b14/flock-on-campus-contracts-unis.pdf" target="_blank" >comprehensive review of contracts</a> by WBEZ found that five of the state’s 12 public universities still work with the controversial surveillance technology company.</p><p>That includes the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, the largest campus in the state, and the University of Illinois Chicago, which is in the process of renewing its contract. Southern Illinois University Carbondale even employs a Flock surveillance drone that costs more than $40,000 a year.</p><p>These schools, in addition to Western Illinois University and the University of Illinois Springfield, have spent more than $450,000 on Flock’s services since 2021, records show.</p><p>Flock’s automatic license plate readers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" target="_blank" ><u>use cameras and artificial intelligence</u></a> to capture data about every passing vehicle, including plate numbers, make and model and even dents and bumper stickers. That information is uploaded to a database that can be searched by campus police, as well as outside law enforcement agencies, to see where a vehicle and its driver have been and when.</p><p>College leaders say the surveillance helps solve crimes and keep campuses and students safe.</p><p>But Flock has come under intense public scrutiny <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/08/02/how-police-officers-used-vast-network-cameras-spy-their-exes/" target="_blank" ><u>following revelations</u></a> that police officers have used the company’s surveillance cameras to stalk their exes. Data captured by Flock cameras have also led to <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/colorado/news/flock-cameras-lead-colorado-police-wrong-suspect/" target="_blank" ><u>wrongful arrests</u></a>. At universities like <a class="Link" href="https://actionnetwork.org/petitions/university-of-illinois-chicago-drop-ice-demand-uic-drop-its-contracts-with-ices-corporate-enablers-enterprise-hilton-and-flock" target="_blank" ><u>UIC</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.change.org/p/de-flock-western-illinois-university" target="_blank" ><u>Western Illinois University</u></a>, students have started petitions calling on administrators to end their relationships with the company.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b00000" name="image-b00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275"
