entries.title: ESPN's Dan Orlovsky doesn't hate Bears — his film-study notes prove it
entries.summary: <p>ESPN NFL analyst Dan Orlovsky doesn’t hate Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams.</p><p>“It’s the opposite,” he told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Bears fans might not buy it after hearing his breakdown of the team’s 59-point outburst in the season opener Sunday.</p><p>“That Carolina defensive tape is putrid,” Orlovsky said Monday on “The Pat McAfee Show.” “That’s bad defensive football more than jaw-dropping offensive performance.”</p><p>Fans perceived the analysis as a swipe and attacked Orlovsky on social media, a typical reaction these days. Also typical, sadly, was the extent of the venom.</p><p>“When you pop on and you’re trying to do work and all of the sudden you see everybody telling you, ‘Kill yourself,’ it’s like, All right, guys,” Orlovsky said.</p><p>Fandom can be a blinding force and block out the most sensible sentiment, which is the case here. Orlovsky, in his seventh season as a daily ESPN contributor, is one of the most studious analysts in the business, thanks to film study that kept him in the league for 12 years as a backup quarterback.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-2f0000" name="image-2f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c83d630/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F77%2F995701c3424b9e8b16cfafbb6db1%2Fjg2-7357.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7daa315/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F77%2F995701c3424b9e8b16cfafbb6db1%2Fjg2-7357.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/92b9bef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F77%2F995701c3424b9e8b16cfafbb6db1%2Fjg2-7357.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Laura Rutledge (from left), Dan Orlovsky, Mina Kimes and Marcus Spears appear on the set of "NFL Live" before the Broncos-Chiefs game Monday. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/92b9bef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F77%2F995701c3424b9e8b16cfafbb6db1%2Fjg2-7357.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/43138a3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F77%2F995701c3424b9e8b16cfafbb6db1%2Fjg2-7357.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/92b9bef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5392x3026+0+283/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F24%2F77%2F995701c3424b9e8b16cfafbb6db1%2Fjg2-7357.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Laura Rutledge (from left), Dan Orlovsky, Mina Kimes and Marcus Spears appear on the set of “NFL Live” before the Broncos-Chiefs game Monday. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joshua R. Gateley/ESPN Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Orlovsky said he learned how to study game tape in high school, in Shelton, Connecticut. Admittedly not the most athletic person, Orlovsky said he needed to study opposing team’s “tells and tendencies” to play at the level he aspired to.</p><p>In college at Connecticut, Orlovsky knew the opposition would be the more talented team most of the time. The way to close that gap was for him to study defenses. The Huskies called much of their offense at the line of scrimmage, so Orlovsky often would audible to a different play.</p><p>After the Lions picked him in the fifth round of the 2005 NFL Draft, Orlovsky maintained his study habits.</p><p>“That is the main reason how I stayed in the NFL,” he said. “I often tell people the biggest challenge of being a backup quarterback is, I’m the only person on the team that doesn’t get game day to prove my worth. So how do you prove your worth? Studying the tape.”</p><p>Orlovsky shared what he learned with not only the starting quarterback, but wide receivers, tight ends, offensive linemen, anyone who needed or wanted help. Now he does it on TV for everyone. He’ll analyze every game each week, keeping notes in a five-subject notebook.</p><p>Which brings us to the Bears’ game against the Panthers. Under the heading “CAR D,” for Carolina defense, Orlovsky had listed, among other observations:</p><p>• First quarter, 3:01, blown coverage</p><p>• Second quarter, 14:48, blown coverage</p><p>• Fourth quarter, 8:51, blown coverage</p><p>All resulted in Bears gains of double-digit yardage, the first being a 47-yard pass from Williams to Rome Odunze. But Orlovsky also had these notes listed under “CHI O,” for Chicago offense:</p><p>• First quarter, 9:49, phenomenal timing</p><p>• First quarter, 9:23, efficient play</p><p>• First quarter, 8:51, great job not throwing</p><p>The results: A Williams 15-yard pass to Luther Burden, a seven-yard pass to Kalif Raymond and a Williams scramble for six yards.</p><p>See? He doesn’t hate Williams. He doesn’t hate the Bears.</p><p>“They were awesome,” Orlovsky said. “I thought Caleb was awesome.”</p><p>His point was, while any team scoring that many points performed at a high level, it more than likely benefitted from some low-level defense. <b> </b></p><p>“I’m not trying to be an a-hole,” Orlovsky said. “I’m really not.”</p><p>Orlovsky slowed the roll most national NFL observers were on after the Bears’ performance, offering a well-reasoned yet singular point of view. As for fans, they’re going to be fans.</p><p>“Trust me, I played in Detroit, so I get that the fan base is so passionate,” he said. “But you’ve got to have courage to say things that your eyes tell you. And I think people struggle with that because they’re worried what people are going to think about them, they’re worried about the pushback from people on social media.</p><p>“No one was waxing poetic about Ben Johnson more than me when he was in Detroit, and certainly since he got to Chicago. I’ve raved about Caleb. Caleb’s an unbelievably talented young man. Did I like [Commanders quarterback] Jayden Daniels more coming out of college? Yes. Is Caleb playing better now? Yes.”</p><p>Even with all the blowback that comes with the job, Orlovsky loves it. He’s a football junkie and a film-watching nerd, badges he wears with pride. And he keeps a schedule to match. He appears on “NFL Live” every day, “Get Up” and/or “First Take” on Monday and Friday and “SportsCenter” on Tuesday, Thursday and Friday.</p><p>Orlovsky will be in Chicago on Sept. 28 for the Bears’ “Monday Night Football” game against the Eagles. It’ll be a busy day. He’ll be on “Get Up” in New York, fly to Chicago and appear on “NFL Live” before the game even starts.</p><p>“I absolutely love it. I’m wired that way,” he said. “It’s a busy schedule, but they don’t pay lazy people.”</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><p>The area college-football schedule Saturday: Illinois hosts Southern Illinois at 1 p.m. on Peacock, Northwestern hosts Colorado at 6:30 on Fox 32, Notre Dame hosts Michigan State at 6:30 on NBC 5 and Northern Illinois visits Arizona at 9:30 on TNT and truTV.</p><p>• All four Blackhawks preseason games will air on Chicago Sports Network, starting at 7 p.m. Saturday against the Wild. WGN Radio will carry the remaining three games. The team officially hired <b>Steve Konroyd</b> to be the late <b>Troy Murray’s</b> successor as radio analyst.</p>

entries.title: Parking meter compromise is a better deal for Chicago taxpayers, top mayoral aide says
entries.summary: <p>A $75 million transfer fee and future profit-sharing agreement <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/15/parking-meters-deal-stonepeak-partners-chicago-city-council-brandon-johnson-pat-dowell" >brokered by City Council leaders </a>sweetens a proposed parking meter ownership transfer deal in a way that nobody thought was possible, a top mayoral aide said Thursday.</p><p>Senior mayoral adviser Jason Lee stopped short of urging the City Council to approve the $2.53 billion bid by New York investment firm Stonepeak Partners to acquire Chicago’s metered parking system for the 57 years that remain on the widely despised privatization deal reached by then Mayor Richard M. Daley in 2008. </p><p>But by claiming some credit for a deal fashioned by some of the same alderpersons who led the budget rebellion against Mayor Brandon Johnson’s corporate head tax, Lee left little doubt that the mayor’s office will back City Council approval of the compromise by the Sept. 30 deadline.</p><p>“There were individuals within City Council who were very adamant that nothing could be accomplished here, that nothing could be negotiated. The deal was ironclad and, therefore, City Council’s best pathway was probably to just accept the deal as is,” Lee said Thursday.</p><p>“Fortunately, there were other voices in front of the scenes and behind the scenes who thought that there was an opportunity… that the buyer and the seller would, might, come to the table and try to sweeten the deal — knowing how egregious the original deal was. Thank goodness that’s happened.”</p><p>With no direction from the mayor, Finance Committee Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) said she and four other veteran alderpersons “took the bull by the horns and did the work.”</p><p>They negotiated an agreement that calls for the city to receive a $75 million transfer fee at closing and 5% of net income going forward — or $376.2 million over the course of the agreement. It also would reduce costly compensation the city is required to pay for every parking space taken out of service either for a special event or construction project.</p><p>Stonepeak has also agreed to sell Omni Air International, which has provided long haul deportation flights for the Department of Homeland Security during President Donald Trump's deportation campaign and explore creating entire, non-metered city blocks as “potential electric vehicle charging stations,” with charging revenues shared with the city.</p><p>Johnson was briefed on the deal, but only after it was done. That, however, didn't stop Lee from taking a bow.</p><p>“A group of City Council members working with the administration — the Department of Law and Department of Finance — has been able to negotiate better terms for the people of Chicago. Obviously getting a better deal than the one they inherited is directionally right,” Lee said.</p><h3>Johnson’s uphill battle with unions</h3><p>Four years ago, Johnson rose from single-digit obscurity to the mayor’s office with millions of dollars and hundreds of campaign foot soldiers provided by the Chicago Teachers Union, as well as the Service Employees International Union and its affiliated unions.</p><p>This time, Johnson's road to reelection has hit a union pothole.</p><p>CTU’s failed threat to take over SEIU jobs at the Chicago Public Schools has fractured the coalition of progressive unions that put the mayor in office. SEIU and its affiliates, which gave Johnson $4.5 million in the last election cycle, are almost certain to either remain neutral or support Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias in the race for mayor.</p><p>Lee dismissed the union fight as a “family disagreement” that he and the mayor were powerless to prevent because, “We don’t control unions.”</p><p>And even if SEIU and its affiliates withhold their support from Johnson, Lee said: "The mayor is going to speak directly to union members and other working people, and that ultimately is what… is going to determine how people vote."</p><p>Lee also denied that Johnson’s decision to attack billionaire businessman Michael Sacks and AIPAC when he announced his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/09/13/chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson-announcement-reelection-bid-2027" >bid for re-election </a>Sunday amounted to an antisemitic attack on Jewish campaign contributors. And he weighed in on the mayor's choice for communications director, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/09/11/five-things-to-know-about-rachel-cohen-brandon-johnson-communications-director" >Rachel Cohen, </a>a social media influencer who attracted hundreds of thousands of followers on TikTok and Instagram after quitting her job at a major law firm and refusing to pay her federal taxes to protest the actions of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. </p><p> With only $630,000 in his campaign fund, Johnson is relying heavily on social media influencers to carry his message around what he calls the "corporate media."</p><p></p><p>Lee was asked whether Johnson has urged Cohen to pay her taxes to avoid encouraging Chicagoans to stop paying their debts.</p><p>"She’ll do what she believes is right," Lee said. “What’s important to Chicagoans is, are we going to have a progressive tax system where those with the most ability to pay are asked to pay their fair share, or are we going to continue to balance our budget on the backs of working people? That’s the conversation they want to have — not the conversation about one person’s tax dispute with the federal government.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-1f0000" name="html-embed-module-1f0000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_78a68fa9-8ca6-41e8-bc5d-0661274c5b39&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml " style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Trump is on the wrong side of AI issue
entries.summary: <p>I’ve covered a lot of elections, and most times, the issues that are going to really matter to voters aren’t brand-new or sprung on them with just two months to go. They’re predictable: the economy, a war, a long-contentious policy fight.</p><p>This year is different. While most voters tell us their biggest concern is affordability, a new issue has entered the chat, taking up an outsized amount of space on the campaign trail, on the airwaves and in party war rooms.</p><p>AI.</p><p>The advent of giant data centers, along with new fears about artificial intelligence and the companies overseeing the technology, as well as the growing issue of privacy and Flock cameras, are all presenting a minefield for politicians and party leaders, and they are scrambling to adapt.</p><p>The issues are so new to voters, in fact, that neither Democrats nor Republicans seem to have a good handle on what their positions are.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-dc0000" name="module-dc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>In Pennsylvania, an important swing state with a number of key U.S. House races in play, Gov. Josh Shapiro did an about-face last month, seemingly acknowledging the growing opposition.</p><p>Just this <a class="Link" href="https://whyy.org/articles/shapiro-pa-data-centers-budget-address/" target="_blank" ><u>past February</u></a>, the Democratic potential presidential contender touted new data centers, promising it would help mitigate the risk that China would outpace us on AI.</p><p>A few months later, Shapiro <a class="Link" href="https://whyy.org/articles/shapiro-data-centers-executive-order-pennsylvania/" target="_blank" ><u>signed an executive order</u></a> dramatically reining in the tech and calling out “predatory” developers.</p><p>Over <a class="Link" href="https://qz.com/data-centers-2026-midterms-gop-republicans-texas-090926" target="_blank" ><u>on the right</u></a>, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott performed the same jiujitsu, at first welcoming a $40 billion investment from Google last year and then pausing approvals for about 1,800 data center projects this month.</p><p>Democrats seem to be settling into arguments over environmental and quality of life concerns, where Republicans are increasingly embracing arguments for more local control.</p><p>It’s undoubtedly a hasty response to a dramatic shift in public opinion this year, perhaps thanks to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.thestreet.com/technology/kevin-oleary-stratos-utah-data-center-backlash" target="_blank" ><u>high-profile case in Utah</u></a> involving Kevin O’Leary from “Shark Tank,” in which public backlash forced him to drastically scale back his development plans from 40,000 acres down to roughly 20,000.</p><p>A new <a class="Link" href="https://www.westernmassnews.com/2026/09/15/umass-amherst-poll-finds-majority-oppose-data-center-construction/" target="_blank" ><u>UMass Amherst poll</u></a> shows 65% of Americans do not want data centers in their communities, and it’s the rare issue that crosses party lines.</p><p>Compounding fears was a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/anthropic-researcher-quits-over-out-of-control-ai-fears-707b7628" target="_blank" ><u>terrifying warning</u></a> from a former AI executive last week that AI could end civilization within a decade and tech companies aren’t doing enough about it.</p><p>Rounding off the trifecta of worrisome tech issues are Flock cameras, automated license plate readers installed everywhere that capture vehicle and driver data.</p><p>None of this is popular with voters. But while both parties and candidates all over the country seem keenly aware of this fact, one political figure does not: President Donald Trump.</p><p>In the past week, Trump has weighed in on the controversies with what seems like reckless abandon in an election year.</p><p>He’s come out in favor of data centers, telling voters that otherwise they’ll be “<a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/31/trump-datacenter-comments" target="_blank" ><u>backwards and poor</u></a>.”</p><p>He’s called fears over AI “<a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-ai-guardrails-data-centers-b85df16775ff7e9611a456b061a0e4b9" target="_blank" ><u>a hoax</u></a>,” likening them to fears over climate change (also a hoax, to him), and rejected calls for more regulation.</p><p>And this week, he said he liked Flock cameras, despite jam-packed town halls full of angry citizens protesting the invasive technology.</p><p>Trump’s been unmoved by public opinion on other issues, of course, including the war in Iran, tariffs, abortion and the Epstein files. And that may just see Republicans lose their majority this November. It’s never a good idea to tell voters they’re wrong about how they feel.</p><p>It’s also not often a brand-new issue threatens to upend an election cycle, and the president is telling worried voters it doesn’t matter.</p><p>Whether he cares or not, the people disagree.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3e0000" name="module-3e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Sky's star-in-the-making Sydney Taylor sees a long-term future in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Times are changing for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" >Sky</a> guard Sydney Taylor.</p><p>The 25-year-old entered the league as a relative unknown, signing a one-year minimum contract with the Sky. One breakout season later, she’s in line for a much bigger payday.</p><p>Not bad for a mid-major kid who spent the previous two years playing in Poland and Lithuania.</p><p>Taylor will become a reserved free agent after this season, meaning she’ll be able to negotiate only with the Sky. Exactly how much she’ll earn and how long she’ll sign for are the open questions.</p><p>The good news for Sky fans: she told the Sun-Times on Thursday that she sees a long-term future in Chicago.</p><p>“A long-term contract would be really nice,” she said. “A couple years. I would love to stay in Chicago and play for a while, as long as I can. I love the city, I love the fans. That’d be a great opportunity for me.”</p><p>It’s an even better opportunity for the Sky. Bringing Taylor to training camp was one of their most rewarding personnel decisions in years. She ranks third among rookies in scoring at 13.8 points per game.</p><p>Once she worked her way into the starting lineup, Taylor averaged 16 points and shot 36.7% from three-point range. She also became the first WNBA player since Courtney Vandersloot in 2022 to hit multiple buzzer-beating three-pointers in a season.</p><p>There aren’t many great shooting guards in the league. Taylor has a chance to become one of them.</p><p>All of this means the Sky will want to lock her in as part of a young core with Rickea Jackson, Kamilla Cardoso and Gabriela Jaquez. It’s encouraging that Taylor is on board with that vision.</p><p>“She’s hopefully here for a long time,” coach Tyler Marsh said Wednesday. “She’s earned that. Her teammates believe in her. The city and this organization is behind her. The fan base loves her. We want to keep her in a Sky jersey for as long as possible.”</p><p>Taylor is still deciding what she’ll do this offseason. The Turkish club Galatasaray announced her signing in June, but Taylor now says she will “most likely” remain in the United States. She declined to comment on what changed.</p><p>Staying stateside could put Unrivaled, the 3-on-3 league founded by Breanna Stewart and Napheesa Collier, in the mix. Taylor excelled with USA Basketball’s under-23 three-on-three team and is just the kind of young, exciting talent Unrivaled typically promotes.</p><p>Whatever she chooses, Marsh’s offseason priorities for Taylor will be similar to what he has emphasized throughout the season: Don’t fall so in love with the outside shot that she forgets about her speed to the basket. He also wants her to continue developing as a playmaker, using the threat of her drives to create opportunities for others.</p><p>Taylor entered the FIBA World Cup break coming off a groin injury and the first mini-slump of her season. But after two weeks of rest, she says she feels “100% healthy” and doesn’t expect to be on a minutes restriction during the final week of the regular season.</p><p>That gives her four more games to cap off a life-changing season.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Northwestern football coach David Braun gets contract extension through 2031 season
entries.summary: <p>Northwestern has extended coach David Braun's contract through the 2031 season.</p><p>The school announced the extension Thursday. Financial terms weren't released.</p><p>Braun is in his fourth season at Northwestern and carries a 20-19 record into Saturday's game with Colorado. Northwestern went 7-6 and beat Central Michigan in the GameAbove Sports Bowl last season.</p><p>Northwestern vice president for athletics and recreation Mark Jackson said in a statement that Braun "is everything that we need in a head coach."</p><p>"He recruits young men of high character who embrace our elite academic environment and who compete in the most competitive conference in the country," Jackson said. "David develops our student-athletes at a time when retaining talent has never been harder, and they choose to remain Wildcats when other options appear. He does it with a rare combination of relentless competitiveness and integrity."</p><p>Braun arrived at Northwestern as a defensive coordinator on Pat Fitzgerald's staff in January 2023 and was named interim head coach later that year after Fitzgerald was fired amid <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/northwestern-hazing-scandal" >a team hazing scandal. </a>Fitzgerald later sued the school before reaching a settlement.</p><p>Northwestern went 8-5 under Braun in 2023 after going 1-11 a year earlier, a turnaround that helped him get the interim tag removed from his title. After slipping to 4-8 in 2024, Northwestern rebounded to earn bowl eligibility last season.</p><p>The Wildcats opened the 2026 season by beating South Dakota State 34-18.</p><p>"I am so honored to have the opportunity to lead a storied football program at an institution that demands and expects excellence, instills character, and provides a transformative experience for its student-athletes on and off the field," Braun said in a statement released by the school.</p><p>Before coming to Northwestern, Braun was a defensive coordinator at the Championship Subdivision level with North Dakota State, which won two titles during his tenure.</p><p>Braun was born in Lake Forest, about 20 miles from Northwestern's campus.</p>

entries.title: Customs officer guilty of using gun, badge to sexually assault women in Chicago suburbs
entries.summary: <p>A federal jury convicted a federal immigration officer Thursday who had been accused of using his gun and badge to commit violent sexual assaults of four women in Chicago's suburbs in 2022.</p><p>U.S. Customs and Border Protection Officer Luis Uribe faces a potential life sentence after being convicted of 10 counts of deprivation of civil rights under color of law<b> </b>and one count of brandishing a firearm during a crime of violence.</p><p>Uribe offered no obvious reaction in the courtroom while the verdict was being read, listening with his hands clasped at the defense table. But when he was taken back into a court lockup, he told someone in the courtroom to "take care" of his family. He has been in federal custody since his arrest late last year.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/16/luis-uribe-customs-border-protection-sexual-assault" >Jury weighs case of customs officer accused of sexual assaults — after prosecutor slams his ‘rape joke’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>U.S. District Judge Jorge Alonso set sentencing for Jan. 21.</p><p>A grand jury <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" ><u>handed up an indictment</u></a> against Uribe<b> </b>in December 2025, in the waning days of the Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign. However, the allegations against Uribe had no connection to the Trump administration effort that rocked the Chicago area.</p><p>Rather, prosecutors accused Uribe of attacking four women in Schaumburg and Naperville<b> </b>between February and October 2022. They said he was even offered free sex if he ended his assaults.</p><p>Defense attorney Michael Clancy told jurors<b> </b>that Uribe<b> </b>was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/09/luis-uribe-cbp-border-protection-sexual-assault" target="_blank" ><u>set up by a prostitution ring</u></a> overseen by a boss in China. Uribe even took the witness stand, admitting he’d visited prostitutes and hid it from his wife. But he insisted he “never raped anybody.”</p><p>Still, when a prosecutor asked him whether he’d used “physical fitness time”<b> </b>to get away from work for an alleged attack, Uribe quipped in front of the jury that he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/15/cbp-officer-tells-jury-he-met-sex-workers-but-never-raped-anyone-then-brags-he-got-a-good-workout-in" target="_blank" >“got a good workout in.”</a></p><p>“You’re describing the rape … as a good workout?” Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan Shih asked during cross-examination.</p><p>“It wasn’t a rape,” Uribe shot back. “It was consensual sex.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/14/luis-uribe-cbp-sex-work-rape" >Customs officer was offered free sex to stop gunpoint rapes, sex worker testifies</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Uribe, 45, has been held in federal custody since his arrest in December 2025, and his trial began Sept. 8. He’d been assigned to O’Hare Airport at the time of the incidents.</p><p>Jurors heard detailed accounts from Uribe’s alleged victims. However, confusion reigned at times. The women were Chinese immigrants who spoke little English and testified with help from an interpreter. At times, they contradicted each other.</p><p>One woman <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" target="_blank" ><u>described an attack</u></a> at a Schaumburg Days Inn, which began with a man rushing into her hotel room after knocking on her door. The woman said he showed a badge, put it on a table with a gun, and demanded her money.</p><p>Then, she said, he forced her to perform oral sex, pulled her to the bed and raped her.</p><p>“I was terrified,” she said. “He had a gun.”</p><p>Jurors also heard from a woman who denied that Uribe ever harmed her. Rather, she said she was dispatched by a boss in China in 2022 to secure a photograph of Uribe, to be distributed to warn her community about him. She said she also delivered a message to Uribe from her boss.</p><p>The message, she said, “was asking him not to harm our girls — and we agree to provide free sex to him once per week.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/10/customs-border-protection-luis-uribe-rape-schaumburg" >In CBP officer’s rape trial, woman describes alleged attack at Schaumburg hotel: ‘He showed a badge’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The woman said she met with Uribe at the Royal Buffet in Hoffman Estates, where a friend of hers took his photograph. After the meeting, she said Uribe followed them to a hotel and had sex with two other women for free.</p><p>That woman admitted she’d lied in the past about who joined her at the meeting<b> </b>in Hoffman Estates and that she’d failed to tell the feds about multiple encounters she’d had with Uribe.</p><p>Uribe denied that he ever had sex with a prostitute for free. He told jurors that the woman threatened to set him up if he didn’t help her and her boss with their immigration issues.</p>

entries.title: Rate Field owners say 'main priority' is keeping White Sox from moving, as Bridgeport residents air concerns
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Sports Facilities Authority said this week it doesn't support a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >South Loop stadium move</a> for the Chicago White Sox, and shares Bridgeport residents' concerns about a new Amtrak maintenance facility that could drastically change the dynamic of the South Side neighborhood.</p><p>The board meeting for ISFA, which owns Guaranteed Rate Field, came a day before Amtrak planned a Thursday evening community meeting to reveal more details about the facility that is drawing ire from residents over noise and air quality.</p><p>Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth have also requested additional information from the Federal Railroad Administration and Amtrak after being contacted by residents and local elected officials in Bridgeport and Chinatown. The senators are asking for more transparency and communication as Amtrak tries to relocate its current 14th Street maintenance facility to what is now Union Pacific’s Canal Street Yard.</p><p>“The residents would like more information about the plans for the facility, its operations, and any expected community impacts, including but not limited to environmental concerns such as noise, safety, and traffic levels,” the senators wrote to FRA Administrator David Armstrong Fink and Interim President Byl Herrmann.</p><p>Leslie Darling, chair of the board of directors for ISFA, shared on Wednesday that the board learned about Amtrak’s plans to house a maintenance facility on South Canal Street between West 33th and 35th streets when plans were publicly released Aug. 14. </p><p>Darling said the board has not yet met with Amtrak about its plan, but noted that a White Sox move out of Bridgeport “would have substantial implications for all of us.”</p><p>“Our main priority is to keep the White Sox right here in our community. However, as most of you are aware, the current lease with the White Sox ends in 2029 and can continue as a one-year option to 2030,” Darling said. “Our goal is to keep them longer than that. But they do have a right to explore other options… We really want to keep them here, and we are working towards that.”</p><p>Darling said the board doesn’t have details of the plan and wants to meet with Amtrak to learn more.</p><p>“We do not have the authority to halt Amtrak’s proposal, but again, we share your concerns,” Darling said.</p><p>Canal Edge LLC — a company owned by White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia — released its plans for a mixed-use development called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" >The Railyards </a>on Sept. 5. Ishbia’s goal is to move the team to the South Loop location when the team’s lease at the publicly owned Rate Field ends. Amtrak is trying to move its current South Loop facility to Bridgeport and Chinatown. </p><p>Amtrak received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://www.doi.gov/oepc/nepa/categorical-exclusions" target="_blank" ><u>categorical exclusion</u></a>” from the U.S. Department of Transportation for the facility's move to Bridgeport, which would allow it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.” There was, however, an environmental review process that included a noise/vibration/air quality review. </p><p>Deb Ahrens, a former Amtrak employee, was among Bridgeport community members who voiced their concerns about the impact of the maintenance facility in a residential neighborhood full of schools and homes. Ahrens said she worked at the South Loop facility and described it as full of “trash” and “rats.”</p><p>“If you ever get a chance, if you can get permission to visit their yards to see how they care of it, this is what will come to our community: rats, trash. And they talk about how they will upgrade security. Please. Too many times I got waved through by a guy reading a book. And at night, you see the trains with graffiti on them. It didn’t get there by themselves, and the rats didn’t paint it. There were people wandering around the yards at night," Ahrens said. "We ask that you please support not letting them come to our community.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b00000" name="image-b00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4e71f85/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5641x3166+0+298/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F8c%2F3316ea33404e9ea50a4345ec4bb9%2Fisfawhitesox-260917-19.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/26b371a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5641x3166+0+298/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F8c%2F3316ea33404e9ea50a4345ec4bb9%2Fisfawhitesox-260917-19.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd8e0d2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5641x3166+0+298/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb1%2F8c%2F3316ea33404e9ea50a4345ec4bb9%2Fisfawhitesox-260917-19.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. entries.title: Man who died days after being shot in Humboldt Park identified, death ruled homicide
entries.summary: <p>A man who was died days after he was shot in Humboldt Park last week has been identified and his death has been ruled a homicide. </p><p>Raymond Hammitte, 38, died of multiple gunshot wounds and his death was ruled a homicide, according to a Wednesday autopsy done by the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>Hammitte was in the 800 block of North Kedzie Avenue around 5:10 p.m. Sept. 10 when he was shot in the face and head, Chicago police said. </p><p>Hammitte, whose address was not immediately known, was taken to Stroger Hospital and died on Sept. 15,according to police and the medical examiner's office. </p><p>Area detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Muzzling Macklemore changes nothing. What now?
entries.summary: <p>I hate to pile on Macklemore, the rapper recently yanked from Ed Sheeran's tour, further muddying his reputation by association. But I kinda like him, primarily for his song <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rXVaq7EdZ7M&list=RDrXVaq7EdZ7M&start_radio=1" target="_blank" >“Starting Over,”</a> an explicit look at sobriety and relapse. I did smile at first listen, because he presents himself as "some wise monk" and a big famous celebrity, since I'd both never heard of him before and — to me anyway — there is something limp and ersatz about white rappers, though Eminem seems to do OK.</p><p>I paused before using the present tense, "I like him" in the opening paragraph. I still like Macklemore, based entirely on that song, despite the controversy over his remarks related to Palestinians. Then again, I have an oddball view on this subject, one perhaps unique to myself — I see it as a highly emotional issue, where people of goodwill believe deeply across the spectrum. So I don't feel the need to flutter my fingers at my sternum and gasp whenever someone says something I disagree with. I certainly don't see how stifling anybody helps. I would no sooner want to see Macklemore silenced than I would want to be silenced myself.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a40000" name="module-a40000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>I also thought before I used "related to Palestinians" rather than "pro-Palestinian" because I don't quite understand how shouting "Free Palestine" in various circumstances, whether from a concert stage, or at random Jews going about their business in the street, is actually helpful to Palestinians. I wouldn't shout "Down with Trump!" at someone wearing a cross because evangelicals tend to back the president. Macklemore-like outbursts certainly don't relieve an iota of suffering in Gaza, or get any closer to a solution to this intractable problem. Maybe it helps the person shouting, giving themselves a big wet kiss of virtue signaling.</p><p>And yes, I know that beside his "Free Palestine" remarks, Macklemore also once went onstage wearing a false Jewish hooked nose and beard. I wear something similar myself, permanently affixed to my face, everywhere I go, so heck, the more the merrier. Mel Brooks once dressed as Hitler and performed a rap song — that isn't an endorsement.</p><p>We are allowed to tune him out. I deleted both Instagram and Facebook off my phone because I was tired of the endless "Punch & Judy Show" on this subject. Everybody's talking, nobody's listening. If I could inject a thought into the slipstream — and I guess I can, through the vehicle of a newspaper column, which isn't quite writing a broadsheet with a quill pen and pasting it to the post office wall, but close — I would point out, to Jews, that the true peril is not from tertiary musicians making earnest speeches, but the U.S. government using your cause to squash free expression. I care about Israel, but care 10 times more about this country, and since there is a risk of Jews being eventually seen as the folks who hurrahed Donald Trump while he ravaged the Constitution, I want to add an emphatic: Not In Our Name.</p><p>As to Palestinians and their supporters, well, I would point out that being the darlings of Hollywood and college sophomores did not help Tibetans, still under the heel of China last time I looked. If your point is that Israel should never have been created in 1948, I can understand that. But it's still there, your feelings notwithstanding. The relevant question is: What happens next?</p><p>Why not consider both talking and listening? Because this killing people strategy is not working, despite its popularity. Nor does yelling.</p><p>What happens next? A phrase I like to toss out. Both sides immediately start recounting the past, toting up wrongs — "Waving the bloody shirt" I call it. They seem to think if they tally enough suffering points, they win. My reply: "No, let's stipulate that the past indeed happened: What now?"</p><p>Both sides raise equally impossible scenarios. The best I can grasp the loudest view on the Palestinian future, there is a magic reset: an empty Palestine circa 1948 rises from the mist, like Brigadoon, and they return to their former homes. Good luck with that. </p><p>The Israelis, quite committed to sticking around, seem fixated on their own pipe dream of compressing the Palestinians into an ever smaller space, lately by hammering Gaza into a fine powder. Though they would say they're blasting at Hamas cells hiding behind schoolchildren. That argument curdled a long time ago.</p><p>Meanwhile, nothing ever really changes — the definition of tragedy. It will, eventually. But it can't until both sides start listening to each other. Yes, they did that before, in the past. But remember, we're in the present now, looking toward the future. Talking is crucial, because wishing the situation away, and demonizing and killing each other, is not working.</p>

entries.title: Youthful Blackhawks' energy convincing Patrick Kane he made 'right decision' to come back
entries.summary: <p>Patrick Kane could look down at his red jersey Thursday — the first day of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks?_gl=1*1t363tp*_up*MQ..*_ga*Mzg2MDcxODYzLjE3ODk2ODQ3NzA.*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODk2ODQ3NjkkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODk2ODQ3NjkkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> training camp — and see the familiar logo that adorned his chest for so many triumphant years.</p><p>He could pick his head up, gaze around the rink and see the same familiar surroundings at Blackhawks Ice Center that he visited so often between its opening in 2017 and 2023.</p><p>But if he looked any closer, the familiarity began to break down. Almost every person he interacted with throughout the day — including everyone he skated past or received a pass from — was not a Hawk the last time he was.</p><p>"A lot of it is so familiar," Kane said Thursday. "And then you get out there on the ice and look at all the players, and everyone is completely different."</p><p>Teuvo Teravainen is the only current Hawk that Kane ever spent significant time with, and they last played together in 2016. He only briefly overlapped with Alex Vlasic and Arvid Soderblom near the end of his first tenure.</p><p>That makes Kane, in 2026, simultaneously a franchise legend and the new kid at camp.</p><p>It's a strange dynamic, but Kane has realized he kind of enjoys that. The young Hawks are also getting comfortable enough to make fun of him, which is an auspicious sign.</p><p>"It's a happy group, and there's good vibes," Kane said Tuesday. "These guys want to be good players. It’s pushing me in a way, too. [I'm] 37, turning 38 and accomplished some great things, but it still feels like there’s a lot left on the table and a lot left to accomplish — because these guys haven’t done it and they’re pushing to do it.</p><p>"It’s encouraging. Because when you make a decision and sign with the team, [you know] it’s going to be something new. But especially the way the last few weeks have gone with the team — on and off the ice, hanging out with them, being around them — it feels like the right decision."</p><p>In fact, there actually is something vaguely familiar to Kane about this team's unity and camaraderie.</p><p>"There’s some similarities with the way we came up in 2007, 2008, 2009," he said. "You’re a young team coming up together, and you’re like best friends in a way. I see that with this group, too."</p><p>Kane has already hit it off with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/08/30/blackhawks-frank-nazar-summer-dentist-patrick-kane-convert-opportunities" >Frank Nazar</a>, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/17/blackhawks-training-camp-lines-jeff-blashill-frank-nazar" >centered his line Thursday</a>. Nazar's ability to be "in the moment" and push himself to improve with every practice rep has impressed him.</p><p>He has already gotten some laughs out of observing energizer bunny Oliver Moore, who somehow beat him to the rink every morning the past few weeks.</p><p>"I’m like, 'I can’t catch this guy,'" Kane said.</p><p>And he has already begun building chemistry with "smooth" Roman Kantserov, who skated on his opposite wing Thursday and showed off his English fluency by asking Kane many questions about what he was seeing on the ice.</p><p>Nevertheless, Kane has 19 years' worth of wisdom that these kids can't possibly have yet. That should be a valuable asset.</p><p>"I feel like I can really help them," Kane said. "[Seeing] the ability and the skill and the talent, I still think there’s another level on top of that if you can, I don’t want to say 'learn how to play the game,' but learn different situations. The way to attack offensively, the way to isolate guys, different things like that."</p><p>The Hawks' coaching staff has almost entirely changed since 2023, too. But Kane does have a preexisting relationship with Jeff Blashill from international tournaments in 2018 and 2019 that could prove useful.</p><p>"The thing I like about [Blashill] is he's going to be hard on me, and he's going to be hard on everyone. [There's] no favoritism," Kane said. "He's doing whatever he can to get the best out of the group, and that's the way it should be."</p>

entries.title: Zoning Committee OK renter protections proposed by Mayor Johnson's Council opponents
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s City Council opposition on Thursday strengthened its hand in the battle to determine how much protection Chicago will give to more than 600,000 renters.</p><p>One day after the Council's Housing Committee narrowly approved Johnson’s watered-down ordinance — minus a “just cause” provision that would have required landlords to make relocation payments to evicted tenants — the Zoning Committee approved a rival version favored by some of the same real estate interests that blocked Johnson’s Bring Chicago Home referendum. The Thursday vote was 12-6.</p><p>Johnson's version would establish a registry to log who owns the city’s more than 500,000 rental units and whether those landlords are complying with the law. It also would create a Bureau of Rental Housing Services to establish and enforce new standards landlords must follow to guarantee safe and sanitary living conditions. And a “Renters Bill of Rights” would require landlords to clearly explain all fees, ban move-in fees and require landlords to choose between monthly and annual pet fees.</p><p>The ordinance includes an annual registration fee of $20 per unit that’s expected to raise $22 million a year to cover inspections, attorneys and other enforcement costs.</p><p>The measure championed by Zoning Chair and 36th Ward Ald. Gilbert Villegas has some similarities, but differs from Johnson's proposal in many respects. There is no registration fee, no rental housing bureau, and an office of rental services would rely on existing staff rather than new hirings. Villegas' version would also ban some junk fees. </p><p> </p><p></p><p>To confront what Villegas says are the root causes of rising rents, the alternative plan sets a 180-day deadline for the city’s buildings commissioner to devise a plan to expedite housing permits and eliminate other red tape standing in the way of housing construction.</p><p>“We want to put forward a path for housing providers and signal to folks that want to invest in housing that we’re open for these investments,” Villegas said. “The stress that is occurring right now in the rental market is because of lack of supply. That’s why our ordinance talks about that as well … trying to figure out how to get a path to predictability on investments in Chicago.”</p><p>Now that dueling ordinances have both been approved by City Council committees, the stage is set for negotiations to start. Within minutes of Thursday’s vote, the mayor’s office reached out to arrange a Friday bargaining session. </p><p>Villegas won’t be going to that meeting alone. His colleagues in what Johnson likes to call the “corporate caucus” want to be there as well.</p><p></p><p>Villegas said he will not be rushed into striking a deal in time for a potential vote at Wednesday’s City Council meeting.</p><p></p><p>"We’re not gonna be put in a position where we’re trying to negotiate something just to meet a timeline that the mayor wants,” Villegas said.</p><p>The mayor’s office responded to Thursday’s vote by saying the Johnson administration is “heartened the City Council is responding to the issues facing renters in our city.”</p><p>“As families are hit with ever-increasing fees and suffer from dangerous living conditions that go unaddressed, we’re encouraged there is a clear appetite to finally update Chicago’s renter protections, and we look forward to continuing to work with members to get this right for working Chicagoans,” a statement from the mayor's office said.</p><p></p><p>However, the mayor’s office continued to contend that the alternative version “falls well short of delivering the relief working Chicagoans need" because it has no “funding mechanism or meaningful enforcement tools,” and includes a “rollback of long-standing protections [that] would leave renters without the safeguards and peace of mind they deserve.”</p><p>Well aware that Chicago’s roughly 600,000 renters could help determine the outcome of the mayoral election, Johnson is racing to secure the strongest protections he can get.</p><p>“At a time when costs keep going up, working families in our city cannot afford to contend with negligent landlords and corporate consolidation on their own,” the statement said, calling the mayor’s Protecting Renters Ordinance the “only option that takes concrete steps to rein in the affordability crisis while providing the city the tools it needs to keep Chicagoans safe in their homes.” </p>

entries.title: Cinco universidades públicas de Illinois usan cámaras de vigilancia de Flock en sus campus, según registros
entries.summary: <p>Mientras municipios, ciudades y universidades en Illinois y en todo el país rompen lazos con Flock Safety, una <a class="Link" href="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/19/43/adaa6cdf4158a9edcceeef346b14/flock-on-campus-contracts-unis.pdf" target="_blank" >revisión exhaustiva de contratos</a> realizada por WBEZ encontró que cinco de las 12 universidades públicas del estado aún trabajan con la controversial empresa de tecnología de vigilancia.</p><p>Eso incluye a la Universidad de Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC), el campus más grande del estado, y a la Universidad de Illinois Chicago (UIC), que está en proceso de renovar su contrato. Southern Illinois University Carbondale incluso emplea un dron de vigilancia de Flock que cuesta más de $40,000 al año.</p><p>Estos planteles, además de Western Illinois University y la Universidad de Illinois Springfield, han gastado más de $450,000 en los servicios de Flock desde 2021, muestran los registros.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-3c0000" name="module-3c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Los lectores automáticos de placas de Flock <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/flock-license-plate-reader-explainer" target="_blank" >utilizan cámaras e inteligencia artificial (IA)</a> para capturar datos sobre cada vehículo que pasa, incluyendo números de placa, marca y modelo e incluso golpes y calcomanías. Esa información se carga en una base de datos que puede ser consultada por la policía del campus, así como por agencias externas de seguridad, para ver dónde ha estado un vehículo y su conductor y cuándo.</p><p>Los directivos universitarios dicen que la vigilancia ayuda a resolver delitos y a mantener seguros los campus y a los estudiantes.</p><p>Pero Flock ha sido objeto de un intenso escrutinio público a raíz de revelaciones de que agentes de policía han utilizado las cámaras de vigilancia de la empresa para acosar a sus exparejas. Los datos capturados por las cámaras de Flock también han llevado a arrestos indebidos. En universidades como <a class="Link" href="https://actionnetwork.org/petitions/university-of-illinois-chicago-drop-ice-demand-uic-drop-its-contracts-with-ices-corporate-enablers-enterprise-hilton-and-flock" target="_blank" >UIC</a> y <a class="Link" href="https://www.change.org/p/de-flock-western-illinois-university" target="_blank" >Western Illinois University</a>, estudiantes han iniciado peticiones pidiendo a las autoridades que terminen su relación con la empresa.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-75d215" class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Archivo Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Algunos estudiantes y profesores dicen que el uso del equipo de Flock para vigilar los campus estadounidenses resulta especialmente preocupante porque las universidades deberían ser lugares donde las personas pueden debatir y estudiar ideas con libertad. Temen que las cámaras de Flock puedan usarse para identificar y sancionar a estudiantes y docentes <a class="Link" href="https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/11/how-cops-are-using-flock-safetys-alpr-network-surveil-protesters-and-activists?ref=404media.co" target="_blank" >si asisten a una protesta</a> o expresan opiniones que las universidades y el gobierno federal consideren problemáticas.</p><p>La gente teme “que sean señalados, que puedan enfrentar repercusiones, y todo eso es realmente, en mi opinión, contrario a los ideales de la universidad”, dijo Torin Monahan, investigador en vigilancia de la Universidad de North Carolina-Chapel Hill.</p><p>La presencia de las cámaras de Flock añade otra capa de preocupación en centros como UIC, que se enorgullecen de apoyar a estudiantes subrepresentados y marginados, porque los datos recopilados pueden poner en peligro a estudiantes inmigrantes, internacionales y estudiantes de color.</p><p>El año pasado, <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilsos.gov/news/2025/august-25-2025-giannoulias-audit-finds-license-plate-reader-company-in-violation-of-state-law.html" target="_blank" >una auditoría del secretario de Estado de Illinois</a> encontró que la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza (CBP) había buscado en bases de datos de Flock en todo Illinois en violación del Trust Act del estado, que prohíbe la cooperación entre las fuerzas del orden de Illinois y las autoridades federales de inmigración. A principios de 2025, la misma oficina estatal halló que agentes de Texas consultaron bases de datos de Flock en Illinois para perseguir a una mujer que se había sometido a un aborto.</p><p>Flock afirma que la empresa ha realizado cambios en el último año que permiten a las fuerzas policiales limitar quién puede acceder a los datos de las cámaras. Pero, hasta este verano, agencias externas seguían consultando con frecuencia los datos recopilados en algunas universidades públicas de Illinois.</p><p>A principios de agosto, WBEZ presentó una solicitud de registros públicos para obtener un registro de las agencias externas que habían buscado datos de Flock del Sistema de la Universidad de Illinois desde principios de 2025 y por qué motivos.</p><p>Las autoridades del sistema dijeron que la solicitud era demasiado tediosa porque produjo un volumen tan grande de datos —y reveló que fuerzas externas de seguridad habían buscado en los datos de Flock de los tres campus más de 650,000 veces durante un periodo de 30 días en julio y agosto.</p><p>“Los policías con los que he estado entrevistando dirán que quieren proteger a la comunidad del campus”, dijo Monahan.</p><p>Pero puso en duda si los administradores universitarios quieren adoptar esa “mentalidad” dada la gran cantidad de consecuencias. “¿Quieren estar del lado equivocado de estas preocupaciones de privacidad y de estos riesgos de vigilancia para el público?”</p><h3>‘¿Por qué estamos recopilando este enorme conjunto de información?’</h3><p>Entre las universidades públicas de Illinois, el Sistema de la Universidad de Illinois es el mayor cliente de Flock.</p><p>UIC tiene un contrato de dos años por $110,300 con Flock para operar 15 cámaras en propiedad universitaria, según documentos obtenidos mediante solicitudes de registros públicos.</p><p>Los administradores de UIC rechazaron una solicitud de entrevista. Pero la vocera Sherri McGinnis González dijo por correo electrónico que la tecnología de vigilancia de Flock les permite “a los investigadores identificar vehículos asociados con delitos reportados, amenazas a seguridad pública y alertas AMBER”.</p><p>Dijo que el contrato de la universidad termina este mes, pero que las autoridades están en conversaciones para renovarlo.</p><p>“La seguridad de nuestros estudiantes, profesores, personal, pacientes y visitantes es una prioridad principal”, escribió McGinnis Gonzalez. “UIC está comprometida con la transparencia, la rendición de cuentas y las protecciones de privacidad en su uso de tecnologías de seguridad pública”.</p><p>Además de su contrato con Flock, las autoridades de UIC acordaron en diciembre de 2025 pagar a una <a class="Link" href="https://volt.ai/the-future-of-campus-security-how-the-university-of-illinois-chicago-secures-a-diverse-urban-campus-with-volt-ai" target="_blank" >empresa llamada Volt Inc.</a> $3.5 millones durante tres años por detección por video con IA de armas, “formación de multitudes” y “objetos desatendidos”, muestran los registros públicos.</p><p>Un portavoz universitario dijo por correo electrónico que la policía del campus contrató a Volt “para detectar posibles problemas de seguridad en tiempo real y alertar rápidamente a la Policía de UIC, ayudando a mejorar la seguridad del campus”, y añadió que los sistemas de Flock y Volt operan por separado.</p><p>La Universidad de Illinois Urbana-Champaign fue el primer cliente universitario público de Flock en el estado en 2021, indican los registros. Un portavoz de la universidad dijo que desde entonces el campus ha pagado más de $180,000 a la empresa.</p><p>Los administradores rechazaron una solicitud de entrevista. Pero en un comunicado escrito, un portavoz dijo que su red de vigilancia de Flock, compuesta por 20 cámaras, “recientemente demostró ser fundamental en investigaciones relacionadas con agresión sexual, robo, personas suicidas o desaparecidas, agresión agravada y vehículos robados, por nombrar algunos”.</p><p>Las autoridades de SIU Carbondale rechazaron una solicitud de entrevista y se negaron a responder preguntas por correo electrónico.</p><p>En total, más de 150,000 estudiantes de las universidades públicas de Illinois están sujetos a vigilancia en sus campus por la tecnología con IA de Flock, ya sea que vayan a clase en automóvil o que los dejen en el coche familiar el día de mudanza. Eso se suma a los muchos profesores, visitantes y otras personas que pasan en coche por los campus diariamente.</p><p>Monahan dijo que le preocupa no solo la privacidad de los estudiantes, sino también la seguridad de los datos. Flock asegura que las agencias locales son propietarias de los datos de sus cámaras, pero esos datos se alojan en servidores de propiedad de Flock, dijo Monahan, y se utilizan para entrenar los modelos de IA de Flock.</p><p>“¿Qué están aprendiendo sobre las personas en un campus a través de estos sistemas que luego pueden alimentarse a estos sistemas de inteligencia artificial y monetizarse por un tercero, como Flock?”, preguntó Monahan.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Former USWNT coach Vlatko Andonovski joins Stars as chief soccer officer
entries.summary: <p>Former U.S. women's national team coach Vlatko Andonovski has joined the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/stars" >Stars</a> as chief soccer officer, the team announced Thursday.</p><p>Andonovski's new team has already been eliminated from playoff contention this season with a 5-17-2 record. The Stars <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/stars/2026/08/12/stars-fire-head-coach-martin-sjogren" >fired coach Martin Sjögren</a> last month after less than a full season on the job. General manager Richard Feuz was let go in May.</p><p>"Joining the Chicago Stars was an easy decision after the conversations I had with ownership and leadership," Andonovski said. "We had the opportunity to talk in depth about the direction of this club, their vision, and values. Everything I heard aligns with the way I believe the game should be played and what the club needs to be successful."</p><p>Andonovski had parted ways with the Kansas City Current last week. He joined the National Women's Soccer League team ahead of the 2024 season and moved to sporting director in late 2025.</p><p>Last year, Andonovski's Current team claimed the NWSL Shield and set regular-season records with 65 points and 21 victories. The team conceded just 13 goals and had 16 shutouts.</p><p>During a career that has included stops with three NWSL teams, Andonovski won Coach of the Year honors in 2013 and 2019. He coached the now-defunct FC Kansas City to league championships in 2014 and 2015.</p><p>"As we've navigated our club's challenges, ownership and executive leadership has been steadfast in their understanding that any future head of our sporting initiatives must be a proven winner with a thorough understanding of this league, its mechanisms and standards, and what it takes to be a serious contender for titles," Stars president Karen Leetzow said in a statement. "Vlatko brings demonstrated experience in each of those areas, and we're looking forward to his impact as we continue to build, expand our sporting structure, and bring this club up to the level of our ambitions."</p><p>Andonovski coached the United States from 2019-23, leading the team to the bronze medal at the Tokyo Olympics. He resigned after the national team fell in the round of 16 to Sweden in the 2023 Women's World Cup.<br></p>
